52
had been destroyed but their loss had not yet been assessed or properly assessed. The
tenant farmers, who lost their standing crops, had also not been taken into account. The
coffee plantations in the tribal area had been damaged and it needs fresh plantation, which
could take many years to give yield. Till then the coffee farmers and the workers, who are
mostly tribals, will not be having the regular livelihood. The Committee also notes the
allegations of improper/ incomplete/ partial enumeration of losses of houses, agriculture,
and livelihood. The unregistered fisherman had been left out and were finding difficult to
get relief. Those residing as tenants were being refused to register their names as they do
not belong to house owners category. As stated by aggrieved persons during the visit of the
Committee to Simhachalam, damaged houses were not being allowed to be repaired or
rebuilt as their houses were on government land and the matter is sub-judice. The slum
dwellers completely lost their dwellings along with their belongings. But the damages to
belongings and other things like rickshaw, auto-rickshaw, pull carts, etc. had not been
counted for. Migrant people who do not have any document to prove their domicile are not
being treated eligible for relief. (Para 3.7.24)
The Committee strongly recommends that the Central as well as State Government
must be keen and sympathetic to the sufferings and grievances of the people. Though, the
Committee would like to place on record the active role played by the Union and State
Governments in conducting rescue and relief operations but the complaints made by the
people must not be ignored through by now many of the grievances must have been
addressed. The Committee, however, urges upon the Central as well as State Governments
of Andhra Pradesh to be more proactive and compassionate towards the problems of the
sufferers. (Para 3.7.25)
The Committee recommends that all the suggestions and complaints made by one
and all civil societies/associations/individuals as indicated in the preceding paragraphs may
be looked into by both Central and State Governments and appropriate action may be
taken, if not addressed so far. (Para 3.7.26)
The Committee notes that schools and colleges have suffered colossal damages in
Visakhapatnam, Vizianagaram and Srikakulam districts due to cyclone and the education
sector must have been facing most difficult time in serving the society. With the crippling
of elementary education and non- functioning of schools, children could be deprived of
Education facilities, thus affecting their future severely. Similarly, non-functioning of
colleges and institutions of higher education may hit the young generation. The Committee
is therefore of the considered view that schools, colleges must be rebuilt on war footing.
The Committee also notes that, as per the existing norms, it is not permissible to assist
an institution under NDRF. Funds may be released under reconstruction plan. The
Committee recommends that the UGC may be urged for sanctioning re-construction of
indoor stadium, class rooms & laboratories. (Para 3.7.30)
The Committee appreciates the work of NGOs and civil societies who rendered
selfless help to the cyclone victims and provided succor to them. The Committee during its
interaction with all such organisations noted their commitment and devotion to the

53
humanity. The Committee would like to take this opportunity to urge them to adopt at least
one village or area of town/ city to contribute for rehabilitation of affected people.
(Para 3.7.34)
DISCUSSION WITH THE REPRESENTATIVES OF STATE GOVERNMENT
The Committee takes a serious exception to the fact that only one team of SDRF had
been raised by the State Government of Andhra Pradesh just to fulfill the provisions of the
Disaster Management Act.  The Committee also takes note of the fact that there are still
some states which are yet to set up their SDRFs. The Committee desires that every state
should form complete and necessary teams of SDRF to face any consequences.
(Para 3.8.4)
The Committee appreciates the District Administration and the Officers, who
rendered extraordinary service during Hudhud Cyclone to bring normalcy in the State. The
Committee notes that repair/ reconstruction in many of sectors is not covered under NDRF
norms. In view thereof, the Committee is of the opinion that there is need either to change
the existing norms of NDRF or additional funds may be provided to State Government/Local
Bodies for bringing administrative physical structure back on rail. (Para 3.8.10)
The Committee is of the considered view that, in the cyclone prone areas, a study
may be taken up for upgradation of the quality of constructions in the cyclone prone cities
as the existing IS 875 Code can withstand wind speed of 140 kmph while the wind speed
recorded during Hudhud cyclone was much more than that. The Committee desires that
houses, electrical poles, communication towers etc, should be so constructed to withstand
more wind speed as has been done in Odisha. (Para 3.8.11)
ADMINISTRATION OF SDRF AND NDRF
The Committee observes that the Manual on administration of SDRF and NDRF
contains the provision that the State Government, in case of a severe disaster and having
exhausted their resources for meeting relief expenditure from SDRF, is required to submit
a detailed memorandum indicating sector-wise damage along with requirement of funds for
immediate relief operations. The Committee notes that under the said situation the NDRF
is only to supplement the SDRF in the wake of calamities of a severe nature. Therefore,
theoretically, there should not be a situation when the State Government is left with no
funds to meet the emergent needs of relief when the disaster confronts the State.
(Para 4.1.6)
FINANCING OF NATIONAL DISASTER RESPONSE FUND
The Committee is in agreement with views of the State Governments that the norm
for expenditure under NDRF be expanded to cover reconstruction and mitigation component
of Disaster Management and recommends that an adequate advance amount be released to
States as soon as a severe calamity occurs, without waiting for the assessment of the
Central team and its consideration by the High-Level Committee. The Committee agrees
with the recommendation of the Finance Commission that the sources of contributions to
NDRF must also be expanded by exemption in Income Tax and also to explore expenditures

54
that are categorized under the head of corporate social responsibility (CSR) for on financing
of the NDRF by amending the rules. (Para 4.2.4)
The Committee also observes that Inter-Ministerial Central Team (IMCT) visits the
disaster affected States when the signs of the disaster is on the verge of withering away.
The Committee understands that there could be some genuine reasons for late submission
of memorandum as in the times of disasters, priority of the State Governments is to provide
succor to the people instead of doing paper work. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that in such cases, on a case to case basis on merit, an advance release from NDRF should
be made to the extent of the entitlement of the concerned State Government of one SDRF
installment which would be subject to adjustment after the assessment through due process.
The Committee suggests that such advance should be considered in all prima-facie , major
disasters. (Para 4.2.5)
FINANCING OF STATE DISASTER RESPONSE FUND
The Committee is of the view that financial position of SDRF is not strong enough
to withstand the damage caused by disasters and the relief/assistance amount is not
adequate to meet the demands of the State Governments to finance the rescue/relief/
reconstruction programs in order to bring back the disaster affected areas back on the rail.
In this direction, the Committee appreciates the recommendation of 14 th  Finance
Commission for strengthening the financial position of the State Governments by devolution
of financial autonomy; however, till the financial position of the disaster affected States are
not strengthened, the States would have to heavily depend on NDRF. The Committee
therefore recommends that the size of NDRF should be increased to provide meaningful
help to the States in view of the rising costs of relief and rehabilitation.
(Para 4.3.3)
HAZARD VULNERABILITY RISK PROFILES OF STATES
The Committee notes the recommendation of FFC that the Union Government must
expedite the development and scientific validation of the Hazard Vulnerability Risk Profiles
of States. The Committee is of the view that appropriate methodology to determine the
quantum of adequate funds for dealing with disasters in different States must be based on
scientific and rational grounds considering States’ vulnerability to disasters. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the index compiled by the Building Materials and Technology
Promotion Council (BMTPC) may be scientifically validated or an alternative rational
methodology be explored at the earliest. (Para 4.4.6)
CONTRIBUTIONS FROM STATE GOVERNMENTS
The Committee endorses the FFC’s recommendation that all States contribute 10 per
cent to the SDRF with the remaining 90 per cent coming from the Union Government. The
Committee hopes that the recommendations of FFC will help in ushering of a new planning
system with the creation of NITI Aayog which ultimately is aimed at institutionalization of
a cooperative and competitive federalism in India. (Para 4.5.3)

55
NORMS FOR EXPENDITURE
The Committee takes note of the concerns expressed by the Odisha and Andhra
Pradesh on the need for upward revision in the Norms. The Committee also takes note of
the observation of FFC. The Committee recommends that the M/o Home Affairs may
initiate discussion with all the States on the need to revise the norms and take appropriate
action. (Para 4.6.4)
LONG TERM VISION ON DISASTER MITIGATION
The Committee observes that only sixteen states have created SDRF. This is not an
encouraging situation when disasters take place frequently and have a toll on the
infrastructure, finance and lives. The Committee, therefore, recommends that all the states
may be asked to created SDRF. (Para 4.7.3)
NATIONAL CYCLONE RISK MITIGATION PROJECT (NCRMP)
The Committee takes note of the main features and objectives of National Cyclone
Risk Mitigation Project (NCRMP). The Committee feels that with the implementation of
this project the disaster preparedness of the states will enhance to a large extent. The
Committee, however, recommends that target fixed for creation of infrastructure should be
achieved in time without any cost overrun. (Para 4.8.6)
The Committee appreciates the launching of NCRMP project which would prove a
land mark in reducing infrastructure loss in the wake of natural disaster. The Committee,
therefore, strongly recommends that concerted efforts must be made by the Central and
State Governments to reduce the infrastructure losses in power and road sectors by adopting
underground cabling and construction of all weather roads. (Para 4.8.7)
GENERAL RECOMMENDATION
The Committee is of the view that financial position of SDRF in both the States of
Odisha and Andhra Pradesh is not strong enough to withstand the damage caused by
frequent disasters and the relief amount is not adequate to meet the demands of the State
Governments to finance the rescue/relief/reconstruction programs in order to bring back the
disaster affected States back on the rail. In this direction, the Committee notes the
recommendation of 14
th Finance Commission for strengthening the financial position of the
State Governments by devolution of financial autonomy. However, till the financial position
of the disaster affected States are not strengthened, the State would heavily depend on
NDRF. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Central Government must
revisit NDRF/SDRF guidelines, for providing adequate compensation to the disaster affected
States. When village infrastructure is totally devastated, it should be deemed that the food
resources of BPL families have been totally wiped out and accordingly they should be
entitled for gratuitous relief assistance, irrespective of the fact whether they have been
shifted to relief camps or not. (Para 4.9.1)
The Committee during its visit to Odisha and Andhra Pradesh came across the issue
that all critical infrastructure like airports, electrical installations etc. are not insured
against natural disasters. This is a situation beyond reasonable understanding. The

56
Committee, therefore, desires that the Government should revisit the issue and explore the
possibility for insuring the Government properties which are built at the cost of tax payers.
(Para 4.9.2)
It was brought to the notice of the Committee that Government properties are not
covered at present in the NDRF/SDRF guidelines. The Committee is of the view that instead
of placing repair of Government properties under Relief Fund, fast track mechanism should
be put in place by the Union as well as State Governments, so that the Ministries and the
State Governments can initiate the repair/ reconstruction of Government properties.
(Para 4.9.3)
The Committee further observes that at present there is no incentive for a State
Government to take up preventive disaster mitigation measures. Therefore, the Committee
is of the view that a scheme should be put in place, whereby State Governments can be
encouraged for taking up preventive measures in a big way. (Para 4.9.4)
The Committee expresses its concern that none of the two State Governments
appeared to be using 10% flexi fund provision under centrally sponsored schemes for
disaster mitigation. The Committee observes that the Scheme was announced in January,
2014 but the same has not been implemented at the ground level. The Committee
recommends that the Ministry of Finance may review and revise the scheme to ensure the
implementation of the scheme which appropriately aims at mainstreaming disaster reduction
measures by undertaking development projects and incorporating the elements of disaster
mitigation. (Para 4.9.5)
The Committee feels that capacity building is a very important requirement in disaster
management, and therefore, recommends that concerted efforts should be made to strengthen
the SDMAs so that disaster management professionals are available in adequate numbers with
due training to ensure all necessary measures by way of mock drills, rehearsals, preventive
measures and planning exercises well before a disaster strikes. (Para 4.9.6)
The issue of late submission of memorandum by the State Government of Odisha
appeared before the Committee during its visit to the State causing a delay in the visit of
IMCT. The Committee, therefore, recommends that whenever a delay of more than two
weeks takes place either from the date of receipt of the State Memorandum up to the date
of report of the IMCT, or from the date of report of the IMCT to the date of meeting of
the High Level Committee, an advance release from NDRF should be made, to the extent
of the entitlement of the concerned State Government of one SDRF installment which would
be subject to adjustment after the assessment through due process. (Para 4.9.7)
The Committee observes that at present the coverage of property insurance in
disaster prone areas is inadequate. As a result, when a disaster occurs, people look up to
the Government for compensation while Manual on Administration of Disaster makes
provision only for relief due to which the daily life and economic activities of the affected
people come to a standstill and remains scarred for a long time. Therefore, the Government
must identify vulnerable districts prone to recurrent disasters like floods, cyclones etc. and
initiate a comprehensive infrastructure insurance scheme wherein all private and public
infrastructure including houses, schools, offices, shops, hospitals etc. are adequately insured
against such disasters. (Para 4.9.8)

Affairs, having been authorized by the Committee to  submit the report on its behalf, do hereby 
present this One-Hundred and  Ninety Sixth Report o n Demands for Grants (2016-17) relating to 
the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (DoNER). 
2. Under Rule 272  of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business i n the Council of 
States, the Department-related Parliamentary Standi ng Committee on Home Affairs is mandated 
to consider the Demands for Grants of the related M inistries, and make report thereon. In 
pursuance thereof, the Committee heard the presentation of the Secretary, and other officials of the 
Ministry of DoNER as well as officers of the Implem enting Ministries/Departments/Agencies in 
its sitting held on 28 th  March, 2016 and examined the Demands for Grants (2 016-17) of that 
Ministry. 
3. The Committee considered and adopted the draft R eport in its sitting held on 22 
nd  April, 
2016. 
4. The Committee, while making its observations/rec ommendations, has relied mainly upon 
the following papers received from the Ministry of DoNER: -

CHAPTER -I 
 
OVERVIEW 
 
1.1 INTRODUCTION 
 
1.1.1 The North Eastern Region collectively represe nts eight States of the North East viz. 
Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizor am, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura. The 
region possesses enormous potential and opportuniti es and also inherent challenges.  However, 
the challenges associated with development of the r egion and aspirations of people of these eight 
States require special attention due to following special features:- 
• The seven States of the North Eastern Region barrin g Sikkim are linked to the rest of 
India through  a narrow 26 km long Siliguri Corrido r commonly known as Chicken's 
neck.  They therefore form an integrated geographical unit. 
• 98% of NER's border is bounded by India's international neighbours. 
• The region offers great diversity – of topography, climatic conditions, language, religion, 
ethnicity and yet has common developmental challenges. 
• Most of the region is hilly and contains difficult terrain. 
• While Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram are overwhelmingly tribal, the 
other four States also have substantial tribal population. 
• Infrastructure deficit in the region, particularly connectivity in all forms is acute. 
• The economy of the region is overwhelmingly agricultural. 
For the above reasons, the Department of Developmen t of North Eastern Region was set up in 
September, 2001 under the Ministry of Home Affairs and subsequently upgraded to a full-fledged 
Ministry in May 2004 underscoring its complete comm itment to ensure development with equity 
for the NER to unleash the potential of its human and natural resources. 
 
1.2 MANDATE AND RESPONSIBILITIES OF THE MINISTRY 
 
1.2.1 Ministry of Development of North Eastern Regi on or DONER, as it is commonly known, 
is a unique Ministry in the Union Government as its  activities are regional and more importantly 
advocating the special needs of the region to the other Ministries/Departments and policy makers.  
The Ministry has been assigned matters relating to planning, execution and monitoring of 
development schemes and projects in North East Region.  

1.2.2 The Ministry of DONER funds projects through various schemes of NEC and also through 
other scheme namely, Non - Lapsable Central Pool of  Resources (NLCPR), to create socio-
economic infrastructure in the region.  The scheme inter-alia aims at filling critical gaps in existing 
developmental programmes/schemes.  Apart from infra structure development in the region, the 
Ministry also funds schemes of Advocacy & Publicity  for showcasing potential of North Eastern 
Region and that of Technical Assistance & Capacity Building for training youth of the region and 
State Government/Public Sector employees of the reg ion.  The Ministry has also started 
implementing Central Sector Plan Scheme titled NLCP R Central in 2012-13 to supplement efforts 
of central Ministries/Departments for development o f infrastructure in the region. The Ministry’s 
Plan allocation has steadily increased from Rs.1019 .90 crore in 2002-03 to Rs.2430.01  crore in 
2016-17.    
1.2.3 In order to help the region to optimize benef its of funding from Government of India, 
review meetings are being organized from time to ti me,   which are attended by senior 
functionaries of the State Governments and the conc erned Ministries/Departments of Government 
of India. Various policy and procedural decisions a re taken in these meetings.  In addition, the 
Ministry follows up mobilization of external aid fo r catalyzing development in the region through 
road construction, livelihood project, etc.  
1.2.4 There are two Central Public Sector Enterpris es (CPSEs) under administrative control of 
the Ministry, viz., North Eastern Handicrafts and H andloom Development Corporation Ltd., 
(NEHHDC) and North Eastern Regional Agricultural Ma rketing Corporation Ltd., (NERAMAC). 
The Objective of NEHHDC is development and procurem ent of handicrafts and handloom items 
from artisans and weavers of the region. The Mandat e of NERAMAC includes supporting 
farmers/producers of north east getting remunerativ e prices for their produce and thereby bridge 
the gap between the farmers and the market and also  enhancing the agricultural procurement, 
processing and marketing infrastructure of the Northeast Region of India. Government is supposed 
to extend Non-Plan assistance to both these Corporations. 
1.2.5 Ministry of DoNER also provides interest-free  loan to North Eastern Development 
Finance Corporation Ltd . (NEDFi) - a financial institution - which in turn  provides credit and 
other facilities to industrial enterprises, infrast ructure projects, agro-horticulture units etc. in N E 
region for promotion, expansion and modernisation.  It also provides microfinance in all eight 
states of NER. 
1.2.6 The Objectives of Ministry of DoNER revolve around the following:- 
 

i) Accelerating the pace of socio-economic development  in the North Eastern 
Region. 
ii) Synergizing the efforts of Central/State Government s/Other Stakeholders for 
balanced development of the Region. 
iii) Integrated & holistic planning for the Region, taki ng into account the heightened 
consciousness of the people of the Region, their as pirations, needs and 
sensitivities.  
iv) Evolving a common approach for all the agencies wor king for the development of 
the Region. 
v) Formulating appropriate policies for the rapid development of the Region. 
 
1.2.7 As per Allocation of Business Rules, Governme nt of India,  this Ministry is inter alia  
concerned with following: - 
• Matters relating to the planning, execution and mon itoring of developmental 
schemes and projects of North Eastern Region includ ing those in the sectors of 
Power, Irrigation, Roads and Communications. 
• Non-lapsable Fund for the North Eastern Region. 
• North Eastern Council (NEC) 
• North Eastern Development Finance Corporation (NEDFi) 
• North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corpo ration Limited 
(NERAMAC). 
• North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms Development Corporation (NEHHDC) 
• Road works financed in whole or in part by the Cent ral Government in the North 
Eastern Region. 
• Planning of Road and Inland Waterways Transport in the North Eastern Region. 
  
1.3 POLICY FRAMEWORK 
 
1.3.1 The Ministry implements work mandated in para  1.2.1 through formulations of 
appropriate policies, and implementation of specifi c Plan programmes.  North Eastern Council, 
Shillong also implements various Plan Schemes in the Region.   
 
1.3.2  All non-exempted Ministries/Departments of G overnment of India are required to 
earmark at least 10% of Gross Budgetary Support (GB S) towards development of North Eastern 
States for creation of both economic and social inf rastructure.  Since 1998-99, annual unspent 

amount out of outlays earmarked for NE Region by no n-exempted Central 
Ministries/Departments is being accounted as accrua l to Central Resource Pool  for Development 
of North Eastern Region which is maintained on prof orma basis by Ministry of Finance and is 
known as Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NL CPR).  Accruals from this Pool are 
utilized for financing new infrastructure projects/ schemes in the Region under NLCPR Plan 
Scheme implemented by Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region.  
 
1.3.3 The Ministry also supervises work of Public S ector Enterprises, North Eastern 
Handicrafts and Handlooms Development Corporation L td. (NEHHDC) and North Eastern 
Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation Ltd. (N ERAMAC).  The Government provides 
interest free loan to the North Eastern Development  Finance Corporation Ltd. (NEDFi), a 
financial institution which, inter alia provides cr edit and other facilities to industrial enterprises , 
infrastructure projects, agro-horticulture units et c.  in the Region for promotion, expansion and 
modernisation.    
 
1.3.4 While respective Ministries/Departments are r esponsible in respect of subjects allocated 
to them, Ministry of Development of North Eastern R egion coordinates with various 
Ministries/Departments of Government of India and S tate Governments for various development 
and welfare programmes/schemes/activities in North Eastern Region.   
 
NITI Ayog and Changes in Making Allocations 
 
1.3.5 After the constitution of the NITI Aayog, fun ds for plan as well as for non-plan schemes 
are directly allocated by Ministry of Finance in co nsultation with the concerned Ministries. The 
Ministry of Finance has decided to do away with the  distinction of funds between plan and non-
plan categories . Earlier, funds under plan schemes were allocated by the then Planning 
Commission in consultation with the concerned Minis tries. However, in the new dispensation, 
there could be discussions between NITI Aayog (to g ive a macro economic picture), Ministry of 
Finance and Ministry of DoNER before the budget is finalised. 
   
Merging of two schemes into Capacity Building & Publicity 
 
1.3.6  The schemes Advocacy & Publicity and Capacity Build ing & Technical Assistance have 
been merged with the new name Capacity Building & P ublicity by the Ministry of Finance.  
According to the Ministry, the merger of the Two He ads Advertising & Publicity and Technical 

Assistance & Capacity Building into a single head of Capacity Building and Publicity would bring 
greater synergy and facilitate in better monitoring  and evaluation of the scheme by the Ministry 
and targeting the beneficiaries better.

2.1.5 The Committee examined the figures of nationa l socio-economic development 
parameters vis-a-vis socio-economic development and  growth comprising details of 
indicators like health, education, poverty, income,  unemployment, population etc in respect 
of the North Eastern States and found that health i ndicators in respect of a few states viz 
Assam and Meghalaya are very dismal. The Infant Mortality Rate (IMR)  in these two states 
is higher than the national average and most shocki ng is the fact that no data is available on 
account of Maternal Mortality Rate (MMR) in north E astern States except Assam which 
records very high MMR, almost double of the national average. The Committee understands 
that high IMR and high MMR reflect extremely poor a vailability of health facilities in the 
area and therefore strongly recommends  that the Mi nistry must procure MMR data in 
respect of other North Eastern states and make all out efforts to improve the situation on the 
ground in collaboration with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.

2.2.3  The Secretary, MoDONER  informed the Committ ee that apart from allocation of Rs. 
2400.00 cr under the Plan Schemes of the Ministry o f DoNER  for 2016-17 an additional 
allocation of Rs. 170 cr has been made under the  S ocial and Infrastructure Development Fund 
(SIDF) Scheme of the Ministry of Finance for creati on and up-gradation of  infrastructure 
facilities, especially in Arunachal Pradesh and oth er border areas in the North Eastern Areas 
against the projected requirement of Rs. 170 cr.   This outlay is outside the Gross Budgetary 
Support [GBS] provided to the Ministry.  
 
2.2.4 The Committee found the allocation for SIDF o ver and above the budget outlay for the 
Ministry unusual and asked the Secretary to explain  under what head this money is shown in the 
budget, if it is outside the GBS. The Committee wan ted to know whether the Ministry of DONER 
was monitoring and implementing the schemes under S IDF, and if the answer was yes, then how 
can the Ministry say that it was not part of their budget.  
 
2.2.5 The Secretary informed the Committee that tho ugh the Budget of DoNER reflects an 
indicative provision under SIDF, the amount does no t have any additionality in the GBS of the 
Ministry as the indicative provision is debitable f rom the Public Accounts. The allocation is made 
by the Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finan ce. Union Finance Minister in his budget 
speech for 2008-09 announced to set apart a sum of Rs. 500 Cr for North Eastern Region (NER), 
especially for Arunachal Pradesh and other border a reas facing special problems that cannot be 
tackled through normal schemes.   
 
2.2.6  The Committee was unconvinced by the  explanation o f the Ministry for allocation of 
Rs. 170 crore under SIDF over and above the budgeta ry allocation given by the Ministry for 
the simple reason that if the MoDONER was responsib le for monitoring of the projects 
under SIDF, it would have been logical to include t he allocation in the main budget 
allocation of the Ministry itself. Secondly, it is difficult to apprehend the fact that out of Rs. 
500 crore allotted in 2008-09, still Rs. 170 crore is unspent and as per the Secretary’s 
admission the Ministry has not been able to spend t he money during 2015-16 too, and if 
unspent, the money goes back to the Public Accounts . The Committee finds the allocation 
under SIDF a classic example of adhocism in budgeti ng and the role of the Ministry in 
dealing with this fund very casual. Therefore, the  Committee strongly  recommends to use 
this money on pending projects or committed liabili ties particularly when the Ministry has 

not been able to grant funds as per the projected d emands and also rationalize the allocation 
under SIDF in the next budget allocation.  
   
2.2.7  The Committee found that the Ministry had asked for  around Rs. 3850 crore as grants 
but was given only Rs. 2400 crore and this deductio n was done because the Ministry could 
not spend the money allotted in the last financial year. The Committee is also given to 
understand that there is a change in the method of fund allocation to the ministries. Now the 
budget allocation is done on realistic expenditure and not on the notional expenditure. 
However, the case with the NER is different from ot her ministries, as Utilisation Certificates 
(UCs), one of the most important criteria for furth er release of grants, remain pending with 
the NE states. As per the admission of the Secretar y, DoNER, and also mentioned in the 
Outcome Budget, UCs worth Rs. 961 crore are pending . This means delay in submission of 
the UCs is affecting the budget allocation and in t urn, it is hampering the growth and 
development in the NER. The Committee in its 186 
th  Report on the Demands for Grants 
(2015-16) had suggested that the MoDONER in consult ation with North Eastern States, 
NITI Aayog and Ministry of Finance may explore a di fferent mechanism like considering a 
different time period (when there was normal weathe r in NER) for assessment of utilization 
of funds and consequent increase/decrease in alloca tion at RE stage. The Committee had 
also advised that the Ministry must continually exh ort states to ensure timely submission of 
UC/requisite documents for timely release of funds for the projects. The Committee 
reiterates its recommendations on the issue of UCs given in the 186 th  Report.

2.6 AGRI-HORTI POTENTIAL IN NER 
2.6.1 The Committee wanted to know in detail the co nstraints, possibilities and prospects of 
agro-horti potentials under the broad umbrella of a gricultural sector in NE region. In response the 
Ministry informed the Committee about the  issues/p roblems under agriculture and allied sector in 
the NER. 
 
Constraints to Agricultural Growth 
i. In the plain areas, small landholdings (0.63 acre p er operational holding in Assam) of the 
region preclude mechanization of agriculture.  
ii. In high altitudes, water run-off is rapid, and ther efore the region lacks water for agriculture 
during the winter season despite having abundant ra infall in summer. Therefore, lack of 
irrigation facilities and absence of water-retentio n practices severely limit possibilities of 
multiple cropping resulting in low land productivity.  
iii. Further, if rainfall turns out to be scanty, then w ater too becomes a key issue in shifting to 
the cultivation of HYVs. 
iv. In the hill, agricultural productivity is constrained not only by the paucity of water but also 
by the fact that land is held not by individuals but by the community as a whole.  
v. Lack of individual ownership rights may be an impor tant reason for the popularity of jhum 
cultivation in the hills.  
vi. The soil in hill areas is highly acidic and to neut ralize it, hill tribes often take recourse to 
burning wood and leaves to increase its alkalinity.  
vii. Further, as land is common property, cultivators ha ve no incentive to invest in it to 
improve its quality.  
 
Crop cultivation: 
i. The diverse geo-climatic conditions in the northeas t make it an ideal location for the 
cultivation of a variety of agricultural crops. Agr icultural systems remain predominantly 
traditional. The land to person ratio for the NE re gion (0.68 ha/person) is much higher than 

the national average (0.32 ha/person), with Arunach al Pradesh having the highest ratio 
(8.63 ha/person) and Assam the lowest (0.29 ha/person).  
ii. This pattern of agriculture growth has remained une ven across regions and crops. NER 
continues to be an importer of food grain as despit e covering 8.8 per cent of the country’s 
total geographical area and produces only 1.5 per c ent of the country’s total food grain 
production.  
iii. The Dependency Indices indicate that NER is highly dependent on imports for almost all 
the commodities, the only exception being spices. C ardamom, black pepper, chilli, 
turmeric and cinnamon, considered to be ‘high-value , low-volume, long –shelf-life’ 
products should be patronized. 
 
Horticulture: 
i. NER, particularly the hill areas, has tremendous pot ential for development of horticulture 
as a major contributor to the region’s economic pro sperity. It has to lead the process of 
diversification of agriculture.  
ii. In view of the climatic and altitudinal advantage a nd the tradition  of fruits and vegetable 
cultivation among the people it should not be a dif ficult goal to achieve provided a State 
specific package programme with emphasis on selected fruits  is taken up.  
iii. The programme should, among other things, provide f or needed inputs, nursery for 
planting material, processing facilities and marketing network. 
iv. The creation of marketing infrastructure has to be an important component for the 
perspective plan as markets provide the cardinal li nks so essential for agro-horticulture 
development.  
v. A modern marketing system for horticulture products is almost non-existent in North East.  
vi. A system that covers post-harvest handling, assembl y, storage, transport packing, 
processing and credit is difficult to establish given the numerous constraints.  
 
Animal Husbandry: 
i. Animal Husbandry is an important economic activity particularly in the hill areas.  
ii. Almost all the people in NER being non-vegetarian t here exists a vast market for meat and 
eggs. However, production falls a short of demand l eading to outflow of huge money on 
import from outside.  

iii. It is evident that the region is deficient by nearl y 50 per cent in milk an over 87 per cent 
eggs.  
 
Fishery: 
i. Fishery sector occupies a unique place in the socio -economic life of the people of NER, it 
being an income and employment generating activity at the primary level.  
ii. At the same time, in terms of water area and climat e, the region has tremendous potential 
for growth of pisciculture.  
iii. The freshwater species in the region are about 274 which constitute about 34 per cent of 
the country’s total stock. Assam and Tripura produce the bulk of fish.  
iv. The present per capita consumption of fish is aroun d 11 kg against the desired 
consumption level of 31 kg as recommended by the Nu trition Advisory Committee on 
Human Nutrition.  
v. On this basis the region is deficient by 55 per cen t of fish requirements which is met be 
procuring fish from outside the region at a huge cost of about Rs. 16,000 crores per annum. 
 
Sericulture: 
i. Since the North Eastern Region’s agro-climatic cond itions are most suitable for 
development of sericulture, it can be developed int o a major income earning and 
employment generating sector.  
ii. North East’s contribution towards the country’s tot al production of raw silk is generally 
about 6 per cent.  
iii. However, its contribution in terms of Muga and Seri production is more than 90 percent.  
iv. Over 3.8 lakh families are engaged in sericulture f arming and annual production recorded 
is 1063 MT.  
 
Bamboo-Based Activity: 
i. Bamboo plays an important part in the lives of the people of the NE States. It is an integral 
part of the socio-cultural and economic traditions of the region. Bamboo grows in natural 
forests, and is cultivated in homesteads, groves an d on private plantations. More than 60 
per cent of country’s bamboo resources are availabl e in the NE States and 20 per cent of 
the world’s resources are grown in the region. 

ii. At present, the volume of bamboo production falls s hort of national demand. The current 
demand for bamboo in India is estimated at 28 milli on tones, only half of which is 
presently available. So there is a need to improve the productivity of bamboo in the NE 
States, since more than 60 per cent of the bamboo resources are available here.  
iii. A number of initiatives have been taken by the Nati onal Mission on Bamboo Application 
(NMBA) to develop the bamboo sector in NER. Provisi ons have been made to arrange 
finance for bamboo development from the Technology Information Forecasting & 
Assessment Council (TIFAC), the National Mission on  Bamboo Applications, NEC, 
NEDFi and other banks.  
 
Major constraints in Agro-processing industry in the NER: 
i. Virtually no effective processing industry. 
ii. Suffering from both supply and demand problems, agr o-processing industries are grossly 
underutilized and incur losses. 
iii. Geographical isolation involving high transport costs on materials and final product. 
iv. Inadequate working capital. 
v. Poor marketing strategies with an absence of marketing networks. 
vi. Lack of market intelligence, absence of sales promotion and  
vii. Inability to compete with established brand names d ue to comparatively lower and 
uncertain quality. 
 
Certain Gaps Identified in Coffee Development in NER: 
The coffee development programme has been taken up in a scattered manner across all States of 
NER. Some gaps identified are: 
i. There is lack of adequate technical manpower to take up development activities. 
ii. Lack of involvement by concerned State agencies. 
iii. Inadequate adoption of technology by growers due to socio-economic reasons. 
iv. Poor accessibility and security issues. 
v. Long gestation period of coffee requiring sustained  investments and involvement which is 
a deterrent to tribal growers. 
vi. Only Coffee Board’s support (Rs 15,000/ha) remains insufficient to attract growers for 
consolidation activity. 

vii. Inclement weather coinciding with harvest contributing to the deterioration of quality. 
viii. Inadequate processing and marketing facilities. 
ix. Diseases/disorders specific to NER (black bean). 
 
Major Constraints for Rubber Development in NER: 
i. There are operational difficulties due to insufficient manpower 
ii. There is insufficient supply of planting material, remoteness of planting locations and poor 
communication facilities. 
iii. There has been extension to staff reduction over the last 10 years.  
iv. Frequent eruption of socio-political disturbances and militancy are other constrains. 
 
Climate: 
i. NER’s climatic conditions offer vast scope for promoting production of spices, particularly 
high value organic spices. Spices the lakadong turm eric, bird eye chilli and ginger grown 
in NER have high intrinsic value and hold vast industrial and pharmaceutical potential.  
ii. There is great scope in promoting production of org anic spices in these States by 
popularizing organic farming practices among grower s. Various schemes are being 
implemented by the Spice Board in NE States. 
 
Major Problems in Spices production include: 
i. Lack of active support from the State horti/agri departments 
ii. Non-availability of quality planting materials 
iii. Inadequate knowledge on better post-harvest practices 
iv. Lack of adequate infrastructure for quality testing, packing and storage 
v. Non-availability of organic certification facilities 
 
Land use: 
i. Forest resources generally represent over 50% of th e land area. Overall, 42% is classified 
as dense forest and 58% as open forest. Around 33% of the land area is under jhum 
cultivation, of which 18% is under current jhum. Fo rest cover has declined dramatically 
over the years.  

ii. The majority of forest land is in community ownersh ip or under the control of the 
autonomous district councils. Women and marginalize d groups have a higher dependency 
on forest resources and there is need to target the m in awareness raising, improving skills 
and promoting better livelihood technologies in forestry activities. 
 
Land tenure: 
i. Land within the NER is in the customary ownership o f the communities and clans with a 
variety of arrangement among the different tribal g roups for the allocation of different 
types of land to clan members by Chiefs, village headman, village councils, etc.  
ii. The emergence of private rights over land has contr ibuted to the concentration of land, 
particularly the better land, in the hands of a few  affluent persons within the community 
disturbing the former egalitarian character of tribal society.  
 
Farming systems:   
i. Farming systems comprise a mix of jhum (shifting) c ultivation on the hill slopes and 
settled cultivation on terraces on the lower slopes  and on the narrow valley bottoms and 
flood plains. The cropping pattern on jhum land rep resents a complex mix of intercrops 
with broadcast upland rice the dominant crop accoun ting for 70-85% of the planted area. 
Yields from the jhum are very low.  
ii. Settled agriculture on terraces and valley land is dominated by rice cultivation. Technology 
is backward with limited use of HYV and fertilizer and yields are low at 1.2-1.5 mt/ha.  
 
Credit: 
i. The virtual lack of credit facilities in NER has re presented a major constraint to the 
promotion of development activities. As a result of  the inadequacies of the formal credit 
system, communities remain dependent on informal so urces of credit, obtained from 
relatives/friends and traders/money-lenders, for bo th consumption and productive 
purposes. Interest rates are very high.  
ii. A number of significant changes have taken place in  the credit scene in the past year. 
Whilst the formal credit system remains largely unr esponsive, self-managed savings and 
credit self-help groups (SHGs) which are becoming p revalent in the rest of the India have 
begun to emerge in the NER, promoted by various NGOs.  

 
 
Priorities & thrust Areas in Agriculture 
i. A state and region specific land use policy suitabl e to different States of the region: the 
Agro-climatic Zonal planning for agriculture sector  prepared by the planning Commission 
may be considered for adoption. 
ii. Efficient extension service: The extension service that is available at present is one of the 
weakest links in agriculture development programme.  The Green Revolution made little 
impact in the North East due to a number of factors , the chief one being lack of proper 
extension network. The farmers remain uninformed ab out new methods and new 
technologies. 
iii. Institutions of appropriate level for agricultural education in all the States to train local 
farmers in knowledge and livelihood. 
iv. A workable policy for improvement of shifting culti vation through material and 
technological input support to ensure optical utili zation of Jhum lands. Such a policy to be 
evolved in consultation with the farming community. 
v. Dairying as an option to on-land farming and better animal healthcare services. 
vi. Intensive as well as extensive development of pisci-culture on scientific basis. 
vii. Make region marginally surplus in food production b y introducing integrated modern 
agricultural methods and developing agriculture horizontally and vertically 
viii. Land reforms must be undertaken 
ix. Promote horticulture on massive scale and increase area under horticulture 
x. Create efficient market infrastructure through a regional master plan 
xi. Use self-help groups as tools of change in the sector 
xii. Raised production of meat, milk and eggs.  
 
2.6.2 The Committee fully agrees with constraints  outlined by the Ministry in the above 
mentioned paragraphs especially the problems viz. l ack of effective processing industries in the 
region; Geographical isolation involving high trans port costs on materials and final product; 
Inadequate working capital; Poor marketing strategi es with an absence of marketing networks; 
lack of market intelligence, absence of sales promo tion and inability to compete with established 
brand names due to comparatively lower and uncertain quality etc.  

2.6.3 The Committee is of the strong view that the NERAMAC, which is supposed to create 
all that is lacking in promoting agro-horti products of the North East Region, has failed in its 
mandate. However, the MoDONER cannot run away from sharing the responsibility in the 
failure. The Committee therefore recommends with al l its might to the MoDONER to not 
only empower and strengthen the NERAMAC to function  to its expectations for the 
betterment of the region in terms of creating marke ting avenues for the products but also 
rope in other ministries/departments and NEC to hel p the region to realize its full potential 
in agro-horti industries.

2.9 NORTH EAST ROAD PROJECTS 
 
2.9.1 In the entire North east Region road is its l ifeline as due to its hilly terrain rail has a very

the heavy rains during the monsoon damage roads to a large extent and therefore maintenance of 
road becomes a priority sector project. Besides, a lot of area in the NER is still not connected. 
Therefore, construction of new roads and maintenance of old roads assume significance in the 
NER. In this background, North Eastern State Roads Investment Programme (NESRIP) started in 
12 
th  Plan period. It is an ADB assisted project which envisages construction/upgradation of total 
433.425 km roads in 6 states of Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Sikkim and Tripura 
having two tranches. The total cost of the project is Rs. 1353.81 crore, out of which ADB’s share 
is Rs. 908.01 crore, Govt of India’s Share is Rs. 378.34 crore and State Govt’s share is Rs. 67.46 
crore.

National Highway Infrastructure Development Corpora tion Ltd. (NHIDCL) as the implementing 
agency.  The Budgetary allocation under NERSDS as p er RE 2015-16 is Rs 75 Cr. only.  Since 
NERSDS is a new project, it took time to finalize t he system and methods of administering it. In 
spite of  its final take off during January, 2016, the fund has been fully utilized by DoNER, after

entire funds to the implementing agency. Thus, it m ay well be expected that the budgetary

construction / up-gradation etc. for economic development of the NE states. 
 
 
2.10.6 The Committee understands that road is ‘life line’ for the North east region but is 
constrained to note that things are not proper in t his sector. Firstly the Ministry has not 
provided progress report about the NESRIP Project. It is ADB funded project on loan basis, 
and the loan repayment schedule starts from the end  of October 2016. Secondly, Secretary, 
NEC in his presentation before the Committee said that NEC had not taken any road project 
for the last four years due to paucity of fund. Thi rdly, as per Secretary, MoDONER, there 
are two broad windows from which the Ministry gives  funds for road 
constructions/upgradation in the NER- one is NEC an d the other in NLCPR. NEC also 
obtains what is called priority list from the State  government and make roads. Then they 
make roads under CRS. Then there is some constructi on under PMGSY (Pradhan Mantri 
Gram Sadak Yojna). Besides, the Ministry of Roads a nd Highways is constructing roads 
directly through State Government and now they have  a new corporation called NHIDCL 
for undertaking road construction in the North east. 
 
2.10.7 The Committee is painfully aware of the mult iplicity of organizations involved in 
making roads in the NER. This is giving a very comp lex picture of the situation. NEC which 
is supposed to undertake the road construction in the entire north east region,  does not have 
money to make roads for the last 4 years, whereas, the Ministry of Road Transport has 
withdrawn Rs. 75 crore from the DONER’s kitty and h as formed a corporation. Ministry of 
Rural Development through PMGSY is spending huge am ount of money to make village 
roads and other district roads. It seems everyone i s working at cross purposes ultimately 
giving no results. The Committee is of the view tha t there should be only one authority on 
the lines of NHAI for the NER to undertake construc tion/upgradation of all kinds of roads 
and all the funds should be directed towards one si ngle entity. Therefore, it recommends to 
the Ministry to work out a plan for creating a unif ied command for road 
construction/upgradation in the NER.

direction. Therefore, the Committee recommends to t he Ministry to allocate the funds 
reasonably to these councils. The amount sanctioned  should not be withheld and should be 
released timely to achieve desired targets. 
 
 
2.12 ORGANIC FARMING IN NE STATES 
 
 
2.12.1 The Committee was informed that in line with  the announcement by the Union Finance 
Minister of fund allocation for promoting organic f arming in NER, the scheme Mission Organic 
Farming – North East (MOF-NE) was initiated with th e objective of ensuring better returns to 
small, marginal farmers and landless labourers by p romoting organic farming in a mission mode 
approach and to reduce risks associated with weathe r, climate change, disease and markets. The 
Ministry of DONER informed that the scheme will be implemented through clusters organised on 
micro-watershed basis which is linked to multi-crop ping and associated agronomic practices. This 
is compatible with the precautionary approach criti cal to resource management in the fragile 
environment of NER where climate change effects are expected to be significant.  
 
2.12.2 However, the Committee of Secretaries in its  meeting held on 23.9.2015 decided to 
transfer this scheme to M/o Agriculture & Farmers W elfare  (M/o A&FW) for implementation. 
Accordingly, MDoNER has since transferred this sche me along with its entire budget to M/o 
A&FW. M/o A&FW has renamed this scheme as ‘Value Ch ain Development for North Eastern 
Region Scheme’.  For implementing this scheme, Secr etary, MDoNER will co-chair with 
Secretary, DAC&FW in the National Advisory Committe e meetings which shall be overall policy 

making body giving direction and guidance to the Mi ssion and shall monitor and review its 
progress and performance.  The scheme aims at devel opment of certified organic production in a 
value chain mode to link growers with consumers and  to support the development of entire value 
chain starting from inputs, seeds, certification, c reation of facilities, collection, aggregation, 
processing, marketing and brand building initiative.  
 
2.12.3 The Ministry further informed that after tra nsfer of the scheme to the Ministry of 
Agriculture, two meetings of National Advisory Comm ittee have taken place. Various States have 
submitted their proposals. In the last meeting held  on 17 
th  March, 2016, it has been decided to 
allocate entire budget amount of Rs. 125 crore to t he States on the condition that money be spent 
after the State Advisory Committee’s meetings have taken place. Since the scheme is for three 
years with budgeted amount of Rs 400 crore, normative allocation ratio among the states would be 
maintained. The Ministry of DoNER has also requeste d all the State Governments to expedite the 
procedural formalities at their end. The Ministry o f Agriculture has also been requested to explore 
the possibility of roping in NERAMAC for marketing in the proposes Value Chain of the organic 
products under the scheme.  
2.12.4  The  Committee has been given to understand that initial ly the Scheme was with the 
Mo DONER, but later on it has been decided to be br ought under the control of MoA&FW. 
In this changed structure the Secretary of MoDONER will co-chair the meetings on the issue 
of Organic Value Chain, however, the controlling Mi nistry would be the MoA&FW. The 
Committee is surprised to note that while transferr ing the entire budget to the MoA&FW, 
the Committee of Secretaries has not even listed th e reasons for doing so. It is also not clear 
whether it has the approval of the Cabinet. The who le exercise gives a feeling of messing up 
of the entire scheme. The Committee, therefore, is forced to observe that MoDONER has 
been sidelined in this episode whereas it is suppos ed to be the nodal ministry, hence 
recommends strongly that responsibility to monitor the scheme should rest with the 
MoDONER as envisaged originally.

3.1 NON-LAPSABLE CENTRAL POOL OF RESOURCES FOR NER 
 
3.1.1 In October 1996, the then Prime Minister anno unced “New Initiatives for North Eastern 
Region” and stipulated that at least 10% of the Bud get(s) of the Central Ministries/Department 
will be earmarked for the development of North East ern States. A proposal was mooted by the 
Planning Commission to the Cabinet for constitution  of such a Central Pool of Resources. The 
Cabinet approved the approach, in principle, on 15th December, 1997.  
 
3.1.2 The Prime Minister convened a Meeting of the Chief Ministers of the North Eastern States 
on 8th May 1998 when, inter alia, it was indicated that a Non-lapsable Central Pool of Resources 
for the funding of specific projects in these State s would be created. The relevant paragraph from 
the Prime Minister’s speech reads as under:  
 
“We are examining the feasibility of creating a Cen tral Pool of Resources 
(CPR) which, in turn, will give critical additional  support for an 
accelerated implementation of projects in the entir e region. This pool, 
created from the unspent balance of the allocated e xpenditure of 10% of 
the budgets of the concerned Central Ministries, co uld well amount to 
around Rs.1500 crore annually.”         
   
3.1.3 This commitment of the Government was also re flected in the Speech of the Finance 
Minister while presenting the Union Budget for the year, 1998-99. The relevant paragraphs from 
the Budget Speech reads “Furthermore, it has been decided that a non-lapsab le Central 
Resources Pool will be created for deposit of funds  from all Ministries where the plan expenditure 
on the North Eastern Region is less than 10 per cen t of the total plan allocation of the Ministry. 
The difference between 10 per cent of the allocatio n and the actual expenditure incurred on the 
North Eastern Region will be transferred to the Cen tral Pool, which will be used for funding 
specific programmes for economic and social upliftment of the North Eastern States .”  
            
3.1.4 Further, as part of the budget proposals 1998 -99, it was announced that: “It has been 
decided that all Central Ministries/Departments sho uld earmark at least 10% of their budget for 
specific programme of development in the North East ern Region. To the extent of shortfall in the 
utilization of this provision by any Ministry/Depar tment (except some exempted ones) according 
to this norm, the amount would be transferred to a new Reserve Fund in the Public Account titled 
‘Central Resource Pool for development of North Eas tern Region’. Presently, a token provision of 
Rs.1 crore is being made for transfer to the fund. In Budget 1997-98, such short provision was 

assessed to be about Rs.1,600 crore. A similar exer cise for analyzing the provisions in Central 
Plan specific to the North Eastern Region in Budget  1998-99 would be carried out and the 
Resources Pool would be enhanced at Revised Estimat es stage to the extent of shortfall from the 
10% norm.”  
 
3.1.5 The Union Budget 1998-99 was voted and passed  by Parliament. With that, the Non-
lapsable Central Pool of Resources was constituted with approval of Parliament. In the conference 
of Governors and Chief Ministers of the North Easte rn States and Sikkim held in January 2000 at 
Shillong the Prime Minister stated the objectives o f the Non-lapsable Central Pool of Resources 
which reads as “My Government has also created a po ol of non-lapsable funds for the North-East 
and Sikkim. This pool, meant for funding developmen t projects in these States, will fill the 
resource gap in creation of new infrastructure, whi ch is a top priority concern of the Union 
Government…”  
                       
3.1.6 The broad objective of the Non-lapsable Centr al Pool of Resources scheme is to ensure 
speedy development of infrastructure in the North E astern Region by increasing the flow of 
budgetary financing for new infrastructure projects /schemes in the Region. Both physical and 
social infrastructure sectors such as Irrigation an d Flood Control, Power, Roads and Bridges, 
Education, Health, Water Supply and Sanitation - ar e considered for providing support under the 
Central Pool, with projects in physical infrastructure sector receiving priority. 
 
3.1.7 NLCPR is basically a gap funding scheme for c reation of new infrastructure in various 
sectors such as Irrigation and Flood Control, Power , Roads and Bridges, Education, Health, Water 
Supply and Sanitation in the North Eastern Region b ased on the priority submitted by the State 
Governments. The main activities of the Ministry of  DoNER is to sanction priority projects and 
monitoring of ongoing projects, the completion of w hich normally spread over the year due to 
inclement weather, hostile terrain and short workin g seasons. During the year 2015-16, this 
Ministry has sanctioned 18 new projects and funds f or 123 ongoing projects (as on 14.03.2016) 
have been released. These activities will be carried forward during 2016-17.

3.1.18 The Committee is concerned about the managem ent of NLCPR fund which by the 
very nature do not lapse, if unused/unspent, but go  back to the Ministry of Finance. As per 
the Ministry’s information an amount of over Rs. 15 ,600 crore is accumulated in the 
‘Central Pool’ as it could not be utilized. The Com mittee gets a feeling that though it is non-
lapsable, the money is not available to the Ministr y of DONER or in effect for all practical 
purposes it is not available to North Eastern State s. The Committee is of the view that if the 
unspent money is not available to the MoDONER, the entire purpose of creating the Non-
lapsable Central Pool Resources by the Parliament will be defeated and hence recommend to 
the Ministry of DONER as well as the Ministry of Fi nance to work out a mechanism to keep 
the fund at the disposal of the Ministry of DONER s o as to enable it to spend the money as 
per the need. This will help to create robust trans port network viz. National Highways, Rail 
network and aviation so that the communication beco mes faster between the mainland and 
the north east as well as inter-state communication.   
 
3.1.19 The Committee questioned the method of budge t allocation under NLCPR. As per 
the information given, the MoDONER has demanded Rs.  1500 crore from the NLCPR for 
2016-17, but only Rs. 700 crore is allotted. The re ason for slash is that MoDONER could 
spend less than Rs. 600 crore (Rs. 511.88 crore spe nt till 14.03.2016) in the last financial year 

therefore the grant has to be reduced. Since the fu nd is non-lapsable, there seems to be no 
justification in reduction in projected demands. Th is gives rise to the feeling that the  
ministry of Finance is more interested in accumulat ing fund in pool than spending it for the 
betterment of the North east, particularly when the  NER is way behind in infrastructural 
development especially in road, rail and aviation s ectors. Therefore, the Committee strongly 
recommends that the Ministry, instead of saying tha t ‘the impact of reduction and increase 
in allocation would be assessed during the Financia l Year 2016-17 and   a view would be 
taken on the need to seek higher outlay during the course of the year through 
supplementary’, they should approach the Ministry o f Finance to release funds from the 
Non-lapsable Central Pool and enhance the grants to  at least the level of projected demands 
by the NEC and also their own projected demands.  
 
3.1.20 The Committee also feels that the absorption  capacity of MoDONER is not 
commensurate with the projected and allocated funds . The Ministry should first enhance its 
absorption capacity so that it can be able to proje ct for higher allocations and also ask for 
keeping the NLCPR funds under it. 
  
3.1.21 The Committee has noticed a new trend that has started where three central 
ministries namely Ministry of Agriculture and Farme rs Welfare, Ministry of Road 
Transport and Ministry of Rural Development are run ning their programmes independent 
of MoDONER. The very purpose of creating the MoDONE R was that it will be a nodal 
ministry and it will coordinate with all the remain ing ministries, except the exempted 
ministries, for development of the region. This is bound to create duplication of work and it 
has been seen in the road sector. Further the trend  also has to be arrested otherwise in a 
very short time many central ministries may opt for  independent functioning in the NER, 
thus relegating the MoDONER to the background or ma ke it irrelevant.  The Committee 
feels that the MoDONER needs to be restructured for  better coordination and 
understanding. The Committee is of the considered v iew that the role and duties of the 
MoDONER vis-à-vis other ministries has to be define d in clear terms and hence recommend 
for adequate changes in the Allocation of Business Rules, Govt. of India.

OBSERVATIONS /CONCLUSIONS/ RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE 
COMMITTEE - AT A GLANCE 
 
OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF DEMANDS FOR GRANTS 
The Committee examined the figures of national soci o-economic development 
parameters vis-a-vis socio-economic development and  growth comprising details of 
indicators like health, education, poverty, income,  unemployment, population etc in respect 
of the North Eastern States and found that health i ndicators in respect of a few states viz 
Assam and Meghalaya are very dismal. The Infant Mortality Rate (IMR)  in these two states 
is higher than the national average and most shocki ng is the fact that no data is available on 
account of Maternal Mortality Rate (MMR) in North E astern States except Assam which 
records very high MMR, almost double of the national average. The Committee understands 
that high IMR and high MMR reflect extremely poor a vailability of health facilities in the 
area and therefore strongly recommends  that the Mi nistry must procure MMR data in 
respect of other North Eastern states and make all out efforts to improve the situation on the 
ground in collaboration with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. 
(Para 2.1.5 ) 
 
 
TOTAL REVENUE AND CAPITAL OUTLAY 
 
  The Committee was unconvinced by the  explanation o f the Ministry for allocation of 
Rs. 170 crore under SIDF over and above the budgeta ry allocation given by the Ministry for 
the simple reason that if the MoDONER was responsib le for monitoring of the projects 
under SIDF, it would have been logical to include t he allocation in the main budget 
allocation of the Ministry itself. Secondly, it is difficult to apprehend the fact that out of Rs. 
500 crore allotted in 2008-09, still Rs. 170 crore is unspent and as per the Secretary’s 
admission the Ministry has not been able to spend t he money during 2015-16 too, and if 
unspent, the money goes back to the Public Accounts . The Committee finds the allocation 
under SIDF a classic example of adhocism in budgeti ng and the role of the Ministry in 
dealing with this fund very casual. Therefore, the  Committee strongly  recommends to use 
this money on pending projects or committed liabili ties particularly when the Ministry has 
not been able to grant funds as per the projected d emands and also rationalize the allocation 
under SIDF in the next budget allocation.  
  (Para 2.2.6) 
 
 The Committee found that the Ministry had asked for  around Rs. 3850 crore as 
grants but was given only Rs. 2400 crore and this d eduction was done because the Ministry 
could not spend the money allotted in the last fina ncial year. The Committee is also given to 
understand that there is a change in the method of fund allocation to the ministries. Now the 
budget allocation is done on realistic expenditure and not on the notional expenditure. 
However, the case with the NER is different from ot her ministries, as Utilisation Certificates 
(UCs), one of the most important criteria for furth er release of grants, remain pending with 
the NE states. As per the admission of the Secretar y, DoNER, and also mentioned in the 
Outcome Budget, UCs worth Rs. 961 crore are pending . This means delay in submission of 
the UCs is affecting the budget allocation and in t urn, it is hampering the growth and 
development in the NER. The Committee in its 186 
th  Report on the Demands for Grants 
(2015-16) had suggested that the MoDONER in consult ation with North Eastern States, 
NITI Aayog and Ministry of Finance may explore a di fferent mechanism like considering a 

different time period (when there was normal weathe r in NER) for assessment of utilization 
of funds and consequent increase/decrease in alloca tion at RE stage. The Committee had 
also advised that the Ministry must continually exh ort states to ensure timely submission of 
UC/requisite documents for timely release of funds for the projects. The Committee 
reiterates its recommendations on the issue of UCs given in the 186 th  Report. 
 (Para2.2.7) 
 
INSTITUTIONS UNDER THE MINISTRY OF DONER 
 
THE NORTH EASTERN COUNCIL  
 
 The Committee is constrained to note the state of affairs which might hamper the 
smooth development of the North East Region. As per  the information received by the 
Ministry the NEC has committed liabilities of Rs. 2 220 crore as on 29 
th  February, 2016 and 
they have said that had more funds been allocated t he NEC could have liquidated the 
committed liabilities and made room for taking up n ew projects. It is difficult for the 
Committee to understand the reason for low allocati on of funds for NEC and it is further 
intriguing that while trying to answer the query of  the Committee as to why there has been 
no increase in the allocation, the Ministry of DoNE R has no justification to offer except that 
if they are able to spend the allocation in the fir st six months, they will ask for more money 
in the supplementary demands. 
(Para 2.3.5) 
 
The Committee understands that there is a lot of ov erlapping and a number of 
windows through which the funds are going to the No rth Eastern States. It is also seen that 
some of the central ministries are directly disburs ing funds to the projects in north eastern 
states. Ministry of Road Transport and Shipping and  Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers 
Welfare are some glaring examples as they have with drawn funds from the MoDONER and 
funded the projects directly. The Committee  strong ly feels that instead of opening many 
windows for funding projects in the NER, the Govern ment should channelize its funds 
through mandated institutions and therefore recomme nds for granting more funds to the 
NEC in order to complete its committed liabilities towards development of the area and also 
enable it to go for new projects as per the mandate given to it by the Government of India.  
(Para 2.3.6) 
 
 
NORTH EASTERN DEVELOPMENT FINANCE CORPORATION LIMITED (NEDFI) 
 
 The Committee appreciates the progress made by the  NEDFi in the area of micro 
financing and empowering the women entrepreneurs th rough Women Enterprises 
Development Scheme (WEDS). However, a virtual lack of credit facilities in NER in agro-
horti sector has been felt which has become a major  constraint in the promotion of 
development of agriculture sector. As a result of t he inadequacies of the formal credit 
system, communities remain dependent on informal so urces of credit, obtain from 
relatives/friends and traders/money-lenders, for both consumption and productive purposes. 
Interest rates are very high. Therefore, NEDFi shou ld earmark certain funds for helping the 
agro-horti sector and also help to revive defunct f ood processing units. The Ministry should 
provide all the support needed by the NEDFi in carr ying out its mandate successfully and 
help in the growth and development of the people of North east.  
(Para 2.3.23) 
 

THE NEHHDC 
  
  The Committee recalls that in its 168 
th  Report on Demands for Grants (2015-16) of 
the MoDONER it had said that NEHHDC was a crucial o rganization for providing support 
to the livelihood of numerous artisans, weavers and small scale producers and entrepreneurs 
and had recommended that the revival of the Corpora tion must be completed at the earliest 
and towards that end, the sanctioned amount in the form of equity must be released to the 
Corporation as early as possible. But unfortunately, in the Budget of 2016-17, the Committee 
finds no mention of completion of the Revival Plan,  which was announced in 2013 and the 
Ministry had promised to complete it within two yea rs. Thus, the Committee reiterates its 
recommendation and expects that the Ministry will c omplete the Revival Plan of the 
Corporation without any further delay. 
  
(Para 2.4.4) 
THE NERAMAC 
 The Committee while examining the detailed Demands  for Grants 2016-17 notices 
that there are no budgetary allocations either unde r Plan or Non-Plan head to NERAMAC. 
Even trading turnover data or earnings from the pro cessing done by the NERAMAC do not 
indicate surpluses or profits for the NERAMAC. The Committee in its 186 th  Report on the 
Demands for Grants of 2015-16 for the MoDONER had r ecommended for early 
establishment  of proposed e-auction centres  throu ghout the region in the North east along 
with a centralized e-auction system  with a view to  ensure better and timely returns for the 
producers. The Committee had further recommended th at NERAMAC should put its acts 
together to revive defunct food processing units in  the region with better equipments, 
technical know-how and affordable finance. However, the Committee is disappointed to note 
that no action has been taken on the ground zero an d it feels with sadness that it will be an 
opportunity lost, if an early action is not taken. The Committee recommends to the Ministry 
to take an appropriate action and provide adequate support to NERAMAC in order to 
achieve the objectives. 
(Para 2.5.3 ) 
AGRI-HORTI POTENTIAL IN NER 
  The Committee is of the strong view that the NERA MAC, which is supposed to create 
all that is lacking in promoting agro-horti products of the North East Region, has failed in its 
mandate. However, the MoDONER cannot run away from sharing the responsibility in the 
failure. The Committee therefore recommends with al l its might to the MoDONER to not 
only empower and strengthen the NERAMAC to function  to its expectations for the 
betterment of the region in terms of creating marke ting avenues for the products but also 
rope in other ministries/departments and NEC to hel p the region to realize its full potential 
in agro-horti industries. 
(Para 2.6.3) 
 
NORTH EAST RURAL LIVELIHOOD PROJECT  
  
  The Committee is happy to note that its recommend ations in the 186th Report on the 
issue have been taken seriously and the earnest eff ort has been made to restructure NRELP 
which will definitely help the people of NER. The Committee recommends that the allocation 
may be increased to Rs. 220 crore as per the origin al work plan at RE stage if there is an
