(Para 2.7.10) 
CAPACITY BUILDING & PUBLICITY  
 The Committee observes that allocation under the C apacity Building and Publicity 
Head has been considerably increased to Rs 73.00 cr ore at BE 2016-17 stage as against 
combined provisions of Rs 20.00 crore at RE stage i n 2015-16 under erstwhile Heads of 
Advertising & Publicity and Technical Assistance & Capacity Building. The Committee is 
not sure about the expected benefits of merging these two schemes which have very distinctly 
different objectives. However, the set objectives s hould be achieved. The Committee hopes 
that the allocated amount will be utilized to achieve the stated objectives. 
(Para2.8.2) 
 
NORTH EAST ROAD SECTOR DEVELOPMENT SCHEME (NERSDS) 
 
 The Committee understands that road is ‘lifeline’ for the North east region but is 
constrained to note that things are not proper in t his sector. Firstly the Ministry has not 
provided progress report about the NESRIP Project. It is ADB funded project on loan basis, 
and the loan repayment schedule starts from the end  of October 2016. Secondly, Secretary, 
NEC in his presentation before the Committee said that NEC had not taken any road project 
for the last four years due to paucity of fund. Thi rdly, as per Secretary, MoDONER, there 
are two broad windows from which the Ministry give funds for road 
constructions/upgradation in the NER- one is NEC an d the other in NLCPR. NEC also 
obtains what is called priority list from the State  government and make roads. Then they 
make roads under CRS. Then there is some constructi on under PMGSY (Pradhan Mantri 
Gram Sadak Yojna). Besides, the Ministry of Roads a nd Highways is constructing roads 
directly through State Government and now they have  a new corporation called NHIDCL 
for undertaking road construction in the North east. 
 
(Para 2.10.6)  
 
 The Committee is painfully aware of the multiplici ty of organizations involved in 
making roads in the NER. This is giving a very comp lex picture of the situation. NEC which 
is supposed to undertake the road construction in the entire north east region,  does not have 
money to make roads for the last 4 years, whereas, the Ministry of Road Transport has 
withdrawn Rs. 75 crore from the DONER’s kitty and h as formed a corporation. Ministry of 
Rural Development through PMGSY is spending huge am ount of money to make village 
roads and other district roads. It seems everyone i s working at cross purposes ultimately 
giving no results. The Committee is of the view tha t there should be only one authority on 
the lines of NHAI for the NER to undertake construc tion/upgradation of all kinds of roads 
and all the funds should be directed towards one si ngle entity. Therefore, it recommends to 
the Ministry to work out a plan for creating a unif ied command for road 
construction/upgradation in the NER.   
 
(Para 2.10.7) 
 
SPECIAL DEVELOPMENT PACKAGES 
 
  The Committee is constrained to observe that gran ts in respect of Bodoland 
Territorial Council, (BTC) , Anglong Autonomous Territorial Council (KAATC), and Dima 
Hasao Territorial Council (DHTC) have been irregular and  some grants have been 

reluctantly allocated. The approach of the Ministry does not seem to be in the right 
direction. Therefore, the Committee recommends to the Ministry to allocate the funds 
reasonably to these councils. The amount sanctioned should not be withheld and should be 
released timely to achieve desired targets. 
(Para 2.11.7) 
 
ORGANIC FARMING IN NE STATES 
 
 The  Committee has been given to understand that initially the Scheme was with the Mo 
DONER, but later on it has been decided to be broug ht under the control of MoA&FW. In 
this changed structure the Secretary of MoDONER wil l co-chair the meetings on the issue of 
Organic Value Chain, however, the controlling Minis try would be the MoA&FW. The 
Committee is surprised to note that while transferr ing the entire budget to the MoA&FW, 
the Committee of Secretaries has not even listed th e reasons for doing so. It is also not clear 
whether it has the approval of the Cabinet. The who le exercise gives a feeling of messing up 
of the entire scheme. The Committee, therefore, is forced to observe that MoDONER has 
been sidelined in this episode whereas it is suppos ed to be the nodal ministry, hence 
recommends strongly that responsibility to monitor the scheme should rest with the 
MoDONER as envisaged originally.   
(Para 2.12.4) 
NON-LAPSABLE CENTRAL POOL OF RESOURCES FOR NER 
 
 The Committee has noted that out of total projects  sanctioned of Rs. 14287.82 crores, 
56.87 percent have been completed and the remaining  43.13 percent is ongoing. But in the 
ongoing projects 36.04 percent projects have got de layed. Since, in NLCPR scheme the 
project cost is not allowed to be escalated due to delay, the quality of project is bound to 
suffer. Therefore, the Committee recommends that an y delay must not be encourage except 
in cases where it is beyond control. 
(Para 3.1.12 ) 
 
PERFORMANCE EVALUATION STUDY OF NLCPR SCHEMES IN XI PLAN 
 
  The Committee is concerned about the management o f NLCPR fund which by the 
very nature do not lapse, if unused/unspent, but go  back to the Ministry of Finance. As per 
the Ministry’s information an amount of over Rs. 15 ,600 crore is accumulated in the 
‘Central Pool’ as it could not be utilized. The Com mittee gets a feeling that though it is non-
lapsable, the money is not available to the Ministr y of DONER or in effect for all practical 
purposes it is not available to North Eastern State s. The Committee is of the view that if the 
unspent money is not available to the MoDONER, the entire purpose of creating the Non-
lapsable Central Pool Resources by the Parliament will be defeated and hence recommend to 
the Ministry of DONER as well as the Ministry of Fi nance to work out a mechanism to keep 
the fund at the disposal of the Ministry of DONER s o as to enable it to spend the money as 
per the need. This will help to create robust trans port network viz. National Highways, Rail 
network and aviation so that the communication beco mes faster between the mainland and 
the north east as well as inter-state communication.   
(Para 3.1.18)  
 
The Committee questioned the method of budget alloc ation under NLCPR. As per 
the information given, the MoDONER has demanded Rs.  1500 crore from the NLCPR for 

2016-17, but only Rs. 700 crore is allotted. The re ason for slash is that MoDONER could 
spend less than Rs. 600 crore (Rs. 511.88 crore spe nt till 14.03.2016) in the last financial year 
therefore the grant has to be reduced. Since the fu nd is non-lapsable, there seems to be no 
justification in reduction in projected demands. Th is gives rise to the feeling that the  
ministry of Finance is more interested in accumulat ing fund in pool than spending it for the 
betterment of the North east, particularly when the  NER is way behind in infrastructural 
development especially in road, rail and aviation s ectors. Therefore, the Committee strongly 
recommends that the Ministry, instead of saying tha t ‘the impact of reduction and increase 
in allocation would be assessed during the Financia l Year 2016-17 and   a view would be 
taken on the need to seek higher outlay during the course of the year through 
supplementary’, they should approach the Ministry o f Finance to release funds from the 
Non-lapsable Central Pool and enhance the grants to  at least the level of projected demands 
by the NEC and also their own projected demands.  
(Para 3.1.19)  
 
  The Committee also feels that the absorption capa city of MoDONER is not 
commensurate with the projected and allocated funds . The Ministry should first enhance its 
absorption capacity so that it can be able to proje ct for higher allocations and also ask for 
keeping the NLCPR funds under it. 
(Para 3.1.20)  
  
 The Committee has noticed a new trend that has started where three central 
ministries namely Ministry of Agriculture and Farme rs Welfare, Ministry of Road 
Transport and Ministry of Rural Development are run ning their programmes independent 
of MoDONER. The very purpose of creating the MoDONE R was that it will be a nodal 
ministry and it will coordinate with all the remain ing ministries, except the exempted 
ministries, for development of the region. This is bound to create duplication of work and it 
has been seen in the road sector. Further the trend  also has to be arrested otherwise in a 
very short time many central ministries may opt for  independent functioning in the NER, 
thus relegating the MoDONER to the background or ma ke it irrelevant.  The Committee 
feels that the MoDONER needs to be restructured for  better coordination and 
understanding. The Committee is of the considered v iew that the role and duties of the 
MoDONER vis-à-vis other ministries has to be define d in clear terms and hence recommend 
for adequate changes in the Allocation of Business Rules, Govt. of India. 
(Para 3.1.21) 
 
STATUS OF MAJOR INFRASTRUCTURE PROJECTS IN NER  
ROAD TRANSPORT 
 
  The Committee is dismayed at the argument of lack  of budgetary resources for not 
taking up implementation of Phase B of SARDP-NE. Th e Committee feels that this Phase, 
comprising of construction and upgradation of sever al National Highways roads, is crucial 
for development of road sector in NER. The Committe e recommends that all the projects of 
Phase B must be urgently taken up in the North East  Road Sector Development Scheme and 
the Ministry must demand enhanced allocation for the scheme at RE stage. 
(Para 3.2.4)  
 
  The Committee painfully observes that while the e xpenditure under SARDP-NE 
scheme in 2015-16 was at an all time high and 33% h igher than that in the last two years, 

however, the physical progress was significantly po or than the last two years in terms of 
road length completed i.e. 363 km and 252 km roads were completed during 2013-14 and 
2014-15 at the cost of Rs. 3008 crore and Rs. 3000 crore, respectively, whereas in 2015-16 
only 115 km road were complete in whopping Rs. 3950  crore. The Committee is at odds to 
understand this anomaly and can at best consider th is as poor performance of the 
implementation agencies. The Committee recommends t hat the Ministry must conduct an 
evaluation and assessment study of SARDP-NE to figu re out the reasons and fix 
accountability of the concerned authorities for thi s inconsonance between the expenditure 
and poor physical progress.  
(Para 3.2.5) 
 
 
RAILWAYS 
 
 The Committee feels that Central Government agenci es must intensify its efforts to 
implement the vision of providing rail connectivity  to all State capitals of NER as some such 
projects are still in their nascent stage and some of them are facing hurdles. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministries of DoNER and Railway s need to get their act together and 
prioritise implementation of projects providing con nectivity to State capitals in NER while 
simultaneously involving State Governments and othe r concerned authorities to remove any 
hurdles that may impact the pace of implementation of projects.  
(Para 3.2.8) 
CIVIL AVIATION 
 
 The Committee observes that except in the case of Pakyong Airport, the Ministry has 
not specified any time-frame for completion of othe r aviation related projects. The 
Committee expects from the Ministry to give informa tion with certain time frame and 
clarity and avoid being vague. Therefore, the commi ttee recommends that the upgradation 
works of all the airports in NER must be completed at the earliest and the Committee may 
be apprised about the progress in clear quantifiable terms.  
(Para 3.2.10) 
TELECOMMUNICATIONS 
 
 The Committee recommends that International Gatewa y and Lawful interception 
and Monitoring facility to be installed at Agartala  must be of world class level and must 
operate in a proactive and vigilante manner to insu late the region from any cyber threats. 
All other projects may be completed as per schedule without cost and time over. 
(Para 3.2.12) 
 
INLAND WATERWAYS 
 
  The Committee is fully aware that the Inland wate rways represent the green mode of 
transport and it is extremely important in the NER because of its unique terrain. The 
Committee observes that in the new RO-RO terminal a t Dhubri which is scheduled to be 
completed by August 2016, only 65 percent of the ph ysical progress has been achieved and it 
is unlikely that the project will be completed in t ime. In the scenario, the Committee 
recommends that MoDONER in close coordination with the Inland Waterways Authority of 
India should strive to complete the projects in time. 
(Para 3.2.15) 

 
POWER 
 
 The Committee takes note of the fact that while NE R has a huge potential for 
Hydropower generation but the efforts of the implem entation agencies have not translated 
this in gains for the region and the nation. The Co mmittee, therefore, recommends that the 
Ministry must exhort the implementing PSUs and othe r concerned agencies to accelerate the 
pace of hydropower generation in NER. The Committee  further recommends that efforts 
must be intensified to remove stumbling blocks from  implementation of Subansiri Lower 
project in Arunachal Pradesh at the earliest.  
(Para 3.2.17)

REPORT 
CHAPTER-I  
 
OVERVIEW 
 
1.1 According to the Annual Report (2015-16) of the  Ministry of Home  Affairs, in terms of 
Entries 1 and 2 of List II -"State List' - in the S eventh Schedule to the Constitution of India  'public 
order' and 'police' are the responsibilities of Sta tes, however, Article 355 of the Constitution 
enjoins the Union to protect every State against ex ternal aggression and internal disturbance and to 
ensure that the Government of every State is carrie d on in accordance with the provisions of the 
Constitution. The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) ha s responsibilities for internal security, 
border management, Centre-State relations, administ ration of Union Territories, management of 
Central Armed Police Forces, disaster management, e tc.    While pursuing these obligations,  the 
Ministry of Home Affairs continuously monitors the internal security situation, issues appropriate 
advisories, shares intelligence inputs, extends man power and financial support, guidance and 
expertise to the State Governments for maintenance of security, peace and harmony without 
encroaching upon the constitutional rights of the States.  
 
GOALS AND OBJECTIVES 
 
1.2 The outcome budget (2016-17) of Ministry of Hom e Affairs throws light on goals and 
objectives of the MHA.  According to it, MHA admini sters and implements a wide arch of 
schemes and programmes. In brief, the goals and objectives of the Ministry are as follows:- 
 
/head2right Ensuring internal security of the country; 
/head2right Promoting harmonious Centre-State relations;  
/head2right Administering the Union Territories efficiently; 
/head2right Preserving and promoting national integration and communal harmony; 
/head2right Raising, administering and deploying Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs); 
/head2right Modernizing State Police Forces; 
/head2right Protecting and upholding the principles of human rights; 
/head2right Managing effectively the international borders and coastline; 
/head2right Extending relief and mitigating the hardships on account of disasters; 
/head2right Working for the welfare of freedom fighters; 
/head2right Carrying out the population census decennially; 
/head2right Preventing and combating drug trafficking and abuse;  
/head2right Implementing the official language policy; and  
/head2right Administering the Indian Police Service Cadre. 
 
1.2.1 Outcome Budget (2016-17), MHA envisages that under the Government of India 
(Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, the Ministry of Home Affairs has the following constituent 
Departments:-

/head2right Department of Internal Security (deals with police, law & order and rehabilitation);

Territories and freedom fighters’ pension); 
/head2right Department of Home (deals with the notification of assumption of office by the 
President and the Vice-President, notification of a ppointment of the Prime Minister 
and other Ministers, etc); 
/head2right Department of Jammu & Kashmir Affairs (deals with t he constitutional provisions in 
respect of the State of Jammu and Kashmir and all o ther matters relating to the State

/head2right Department of Border Management (deals with managem ent of borders, including

CHAPTER-II  
OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF DEMANDS FOR GRANTS 
2.0 There are nine Demands for Grants which are adminis tered by Ministry of Home Affairs. 
Earlier there were ten grants; however, from this y ear the grant named "Other Expenditure of 
MHA"  (it was earlier known as Grant No. 56) has been mer ged with Grant No. 46-MHA.  The 
total allocation for nine Demands for Grants of the  Ministry of Home Affairs for the year 2016-17 
in Budget Estimates is Rs. 88545.78 Crore. In the B E 2015-16, it was Rs. 78950.35 crore which 
was increased to Rs. 80614.81 crore at RE stage. Th us, there is an increase of 9.83% fund 
allocation over RE 2015-16 and 12.15% over BE 2015- 16. The Ministry has informed that out of 
Rs. 88545.78 crore allocated in BE 2016-17; Rs. 150 75.00 crore is under Plan allocation whereas 
Rs. 73470.78 crore is earmarked under Non-Plan allocation. 
2.1 The Demands of the Ministry of Home Affairs are  divided into two volumes - Volume-I 
(Demand Nos. 46 – 49) and Volume –II (Demand Nos. 9 0 – 94).  According to the Ministry, 
Volume-I pertains to the Ministry of Home Affairs, Cabinet, Police, Other Expenditure of MHA 
and Transfer to Union Territory Governments with Le gislature. The Demand “Transfers to Union 
Territory Governments with Legislature” covers Assistance to Union Territories of Puducherry and 
Government of NCT of Delhi in the form of Grants an d Loans for gap funding. The Budget 
Provision under the Head ‘Plan’ is decided by Minis try of Finance in consultation with Planning 
Commission. Non-Plan support is extended only in re spect of UT of Puducherry to meet their 
Non-Plan deficit, as NCT of Delhi has a Non-Plan Re venue surplus. According to the Ministry, it 
releases the Grant on quarterly basis and have a li mited role in scrutinizing, sanctioning and 
implementation of the schemes/projects in respect of these UTs.  
 
2.2 Similarly, Volume-II pertains to the five Grant s (90 – 94) which relate to five Union 
Territories without legislatures namely Andaman & N icobar Islands, Chandigarh, Dadra & Nagar 
Haveli, Daman & Diu and Lakshadweep. The Ministry h as informed that though, provisions for 
the Union Territories without Legislature form part  of the Demands of the Ministry of Home 
Affairs, different programmes /schemes are the subj ect matter of the other Ministries which are 
responsible for scrutinizing, sanctioning and implementing the schemes/projects falling under their 
purview. The Administrators/Heads of these Union Te rritories without Legislature have been 
endowed with financial and administrative powers. B ased on the ceilings fixed by the Ministry of 
Finance on ‘Non-Plan’ expenditure and by Planning Commission for ‘Plan’ expenditure, the Union 
Territory Administrations prepare budget allocation s for the schemes against the 
Ministries/Departments of the Central Government wh ich are administratively concerned. This 
budgetary break-up is included in the Demands for G rants of the respective UTs and presented by 
Ministry of Home Affairs. 
 
2.3 Two out of these nine Grants namely Grant No. 4 6 and 48 are directly controlled by the 
Ministry of Home Affairs.  According to the Ministr y, Rs. 88545.78 Crore allocated to Ministry of 
Home Affairs this financial year under above discussed nine grants, has been distributed as under:-

2.7 When the Ministry was asked whether the MHA/PMO /Finance Ministry has revisited or 
reviewed the issue of transferring of eight Central ly sponsored scheme of Ministry of Home 
Affairs merged into an Umbrella Centrally Sponsored  Scheme called "National Scheme for 
Modernization of Police and other forces to the States, the Ministry has replied as under:- 
"Yes, MHA has written to Secretary (Expenditure) an d Principal Secretary to PM 
stressing the need for continuation of the Umbrella  Centrally Sponsored Scheme 
called “National Scheme for Modernization of Police  and other forces” on 
24.03.2015 and 25.03.2015 respectively. As per DO l etter dated 4.11.2015 from 
Finance Secretary to Home Secretary regarding ratio nalisation of schemes, 
action has already been initiated to seek appraisal  by EFC/CNE and approval of 
the Cabinet to the proposed merger of schemes formi ng an Umbrella Scheme of 
Modernisation of Police Forces. The major Schemes w hich will form Umbrella 
Scheme are Crime and Criminal Tracking Network & Sy stem (CCTNS); Inter-
State Police Wireless; Assistance to LWE Management ; Security Related 
Expenditure (SRE) for Jammu & Kashmir, LWE Areas, N E Areas; Modernisation 
of State Police; India Reserve Battalions, etc. MHA  is proposing for inclusion of 
SIS, SRE Scheme in umbrella scheme of Police Modernization." 
2.8 Elaborating on the negative consequences of tra nsferring these central schemes to the 
states, the Ministry has submitted as under:- 
"It has been observed that the schemes proposed to be included in the umbrella 
scheme concern National Security, Law & Order and t herefore require support from 
the Central Government. The group of Chief Minister s constituted to consider the 
matter has observed that Law & Order and justice de livery system constitute core 
national development agenda and therefore continuat ion of central support to these 
schemes is critical. Special Infrastructure Scheme (SIS), was being implemented 
since 2008-09 in LWE affected States for providing central assistance to States for 
filling up critical infrastructure gaps of their special  security forces, which could not 
be covered under any other existing scheme. During the 11 th  Plan period (2008-09 to 
2011-12), Rs.445.82 crore and during 12 th  Plan period (2013-14 and 2014-15), Rs. 
122.13 crore has been released to the LWE affected States under the Scheme." 
2.9 The Ministry has further submitted that accepti ng the recommendation of the 14 th  Finance 
Commission to enhance the share of the  States in t he net proceeds of Union taxes from 32% to 42%, 
the Government has delinked the SIS from Central as sistance from 2015-16. According to the 
Ministry, the Scheme has been transferred to the St ates for giving them sufficient flexibility to 
conceive and implement scheme/programmes suited to their local needs, including requirement to 
bridge the developmental deficit gaps.  
2.10 The Ministry has admitted that the scheme was useful for training, infrastructure, residential 
infrastructure, weaponry, vehicle and any other rel ated items pertaining to the upgradation and fillin g 
of critical gaps for Special Forces of LWE affected  States and therefore, keeping in view the 
importance of the Scheme, MHA has proposed to reviv e this scheme as a component of Umbrella 

16 
 
Scheme namely, ‘Modernization of Police Forces of t he Central Government from 2016-17 in 
consultation with the Department of Expenditure.  
 
2.11 During the meeting of the Committee held on 13
th  April, 2016 while replying to  a pin 
pointed query of the Chairman of the Committee, the  Secretary in-charge of the Ministry of Home 
Affairs submitted before the Committee that  the as sistance to States through Centrally sponsored 
Umbrella scheme has been revived. 
   
2.12 The Committee is in agreement with the view su bmitted by the Ministry of Home 
Affairs that the schemes to be included in the Cent rally Sponsored umbrella Scheme called 
"National Scheme for Modernization of Police and ot her forces" are of National Security 
importance and are vital for strengthening of inter nal security architecture in the country 
and continuation of support of the Central Governme nt to these schemes is critical.  The 
Committee is hopeful that the proposal of Home Mini stry for inclusion of SIS, SRE Scheme 
in umbrella scheme will be considered as these sche mes are vital for Left Wing Extremism 
affected and other troubled regions/states of the country. 
2.13 The Committee is not ready to buy the argument  that merely by enhancing the share 
of the  States in the net proceeds of Union taxes f rom 32% to 42%, the Central Government 
can justify delinking the SIS from Central assistan ce.   Besides, the Committee is of the view 
that increasing of share of the States in the  divisible pool of Union taxes to 42 percent from 
32 percent would not yield the desired results as due to the imposition of various types of cess 
and surcharge in the  BE 2016-17 such as Krishi Kalyan cess, Education cess, Swachh Bharat 
cess, Clean Energy cess etc. which go directly to t he centre's coffer not to the States, states’ 
share in the divisible pool is likely to go down in stead of 42% as claimed.  The Committee 
accordingly proposes that the decision on modality of the implementation of the Umbrella 
scheme may be devolved to the States in terms of sufficien t flexibility to conceive and 
implement scheme/programmes suited to their local n eeds but financial support from the 
Centre should continue as States particularly backw ard states have their own social sector 
commitments.

in Jammu& Kashmir, North Eastern Areas, Left Wing E xtremism affected States 
and the hinterland of the Country.

have adopted a multi-pronged approach to contain cross border infiltration, promote 
economic activity, provide relief to victims and st rengthen the State Government 
apparatus.

insurgent and militant activities in the North East  Region. Priority includes a 
willingness to talk to groups, provided they abjure  violence, seek resolution of their 
demands within the frame work of the Indian Constit ution and come into the main 
stream of national life. Union Government is also s upplementing the efforts of the 
State Governments through various measures such as deployment of Central 
Security Forces to assist the State Authorities in counter insurgency operations and 
providing security to vulnerable institutions and i nstallations based on threat 
assessment.  
(d) The Government is dealing with Left Wing Extremism (LWE) in a holistic manner. 
Priority includes development, ensuring rights and entitlements of local 
communities and public perception management.  Cent ral Government is closely

CAPFs, Commando Battalions for Resolute Action (CoB RA), sanction of India

of security related expenditure  under the Security  Related Expenditure (SRE), 
providing helicopter for anti-LWE operations, shari ng intelligence, facilitation of

terrorism.

2.27 The Committee is displeased to note the under expenditure in respect of many of the 
plan schemes of the Ministry of Home Affairs consis tently during the years 2012-16 (as on 
29 th  February, 2016).   The main concern of the Committ ee is that during the last four 
financial years, the Ministry has not even been abl e to spend the reduced allocation at RE 
Stage in several schemes which is an indicator of u nder-performances.  The Committee notes 
that under many schemes/projects like infrastructur e for CAPFs or for Border Management 
where there are still huge gaps in what is desired and what is existing.  Moreover, the funds 
available have not been optimally utilized.  The Mi nistry needs to gear up its machinery to 
analyze what is the cause of this consistent under- utilisation and take adequate measure to 
plug the gaps for achieving the desired objectives and goals.  The Committee would like to be 
apprised about the steps to strengthen the absorpti on capacity of various schemes and 
agencies. Besides, the Committee has apprehension t hat this underutilization may prove to 
be a valid ground for further reduction in allocation during future financial allocations.   The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs should pay attention 
to restructuring its implementation agencies so that the schemes /projects could be completed 
without time and cost overrun.

Civil Defence 
 
 
3.2.1 The Ministry was asked about measures adopted  for revitalization of Civil Defence during 
2015-16.  The Ministry in its reply has informed th at it is the primary responsibility of the State 
Governments to allocate sufficient resources for st rengthening and equipping Civil Defence set up 
in the area of their jurisdiction.  The Ministry ha s further informed that in 2015-16, there was no 
central financial assistance to the States for revi talization of Civil Defence since all the Centrally  
Sponsored schemes have been subsumed in the State P lan Funds w.e.f. 1 
st  April, 2015. This is on 
account of higher share of allocation to States in the 14 th  Finance Commission, and the states have 
additional resources to carry out the plan schemes and they can implement the schemes as per their 
own requirement.  
 
3.2.2 The Ministry has added that till 2014-15 the Government of India extended financial 
support under the schemes for Revamping of Civil De fence in the country (2009-2013) at an 
outlay of Rs 100 crores and Mainstreaming Civil Def ence in Disaster Risk Reduction at a total 
outlay of Rs. 290.89 crore for implementation durin g 12 th  Plan period.  The Ministry has further 
added that an amount of Rs. 15 crore was released t o States during 2014-15 and since the scheme 
has been subsumed in the State Sector, no budgetary provision for the States has been made during 
2015-16.  
3.2.3 The Ministry was asked about measures needed for revitalization of Civil Defence.  The 
Ministry has suggested following measures for Revitalization of Civil Defence Setup: 
(i) As on date, only 40 percent of total strength of CD  volunteers exists in the country. 
Therefore, more awareness programs, motivational ac tivities and enrolment related 
activities should be planned to augment the numbers of CD volunteers in the states. 
 
(ii) The activities related to training of CD Volunteers , creation of infrastructure for CD 
organizations and involvement of CD volunteers into  Disaster Management activities 
should be implemented for overall strengthening of these organizations. 
 
3.2.4 The Committee takes serious view of the fact that during 2015-16, there was no 
central financial assistance to the States for revi talization of Civil Defence since all the 
Centrally Sponsored schemes have been subsumed in t he State Plan Funds since 1 
st  April, 
2015. The Committee is not satisfied with the argum ent put forward by the Ministry to 
justify scrapping of central support on the ground of so called higher share of allocation to 
States in the 14 th  Finance Commission.  The Committee is unable to un derstand why the 
Central Government in a federal set up is abdicatin g its responsibilities and leaving the State 

35 
 
Governments in a lurch.  The Committee is aware of the fact that some State Governments 
are already hard pressed even in terms of paying sa laries to their employees, etc and it is 
almost impossible for them to manage additional res ources to carry out the plan schemes as 
per their own requirement.  Therefore, the Committe e recommends that the Government 
must continue to give financial assistance to the States for revitalisation of Civil Defence.   
 
Fire & Emergency Services 
 
3.3.1 The Ministry was asked to furnish detailed no te on fire and emergency service in the 
country.  The Ministry in its written reply has sub mitted that 'Fire Services’ is a State subject and 
has been included as municipal function in the XII th schedule (Serial Number 7 of Article 243 (W)) 
of the Constitution of India and it is the primary responsibility of the State Governments to ensure 
safety of life and property of the citizens in the area of their jurisdiction by providing adequate 
number of fire stations, fire tenders and trained m anpower.  According to the Ministry, the 
structure of fire services is not uniform in the Co untry. Fire Services in the States of Gujarat, 
Chhattisgarh, Punjab, Maharashtra, Himachal Pradesh , Haryana and Madhya Pradesh excluding 
Indore are under the respective Municipal Corporati ons. In other remaining States it is under the 
Home Department.  
3.3.2 The Ministry has further submitted that Fire Services in most of the States fall within the 
jurisdiction of local bodies, which are often starv ed of financial resources and as a result the Fire 
Services have generally remained ill equipped.  
3.3.3 Regarding role of Central Government, the Min istry has added that the Centre  has 
supplemented the efforts of the State Governments b y way of providing Financial and Technical 
support under the Centrally Sponsored Schemes, as mentioned below:- 
(i)  Scheme for ‘Strengthening of Fire & Emergency Services in the Country’ (2009-13) 
with a total outlay of Rs. 200 crore. Rs. 176.56 crore were released to the States during 
the period of 2009-2013.  
(ii) Scheme for ‘Modernization of Fire and Emergenc y Services’ (2014-15) with a total 
outlay of Rs. 75 crore. Rs. 30 crore were released during the period of 2014-15 to the 
States.  
3.3.4 According to the Ministry, since the Governme nt of India has accepted the 
recommendations of 14 
th  Finance Commission to devolve 42 percent of the di visible pool to the 
States during award period 2015-2016  to 2019-2020 in place of 32 percent, as such all the 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes have now been subsumed in State Funds and accordingly, State 
Governments are required to suitably address/undert ake all necessary measures for strengthening 
of Fire Services related activities and allocate su fficient funds for carrying out such activities as 
per their specific requirements.   
3.3.5 The Committee takes note of the submission of  the Ministry that Fire Services in most 
of the States fall within the jurisdiction of local  bodies which are often starved of financial 
resources hence ill-equipped.  The Committee also t akes note of the submission of the 
Ministry that financial constraints have also been a major factor for the State Governments 

36 
 
for neglecting Fire Services. The Committee is at p ains to note that the Central Government 
has discontinued Scheme for ‘Modernization of Fire and Emergency Services’ in the name of 
14 th  Finance Commission recommendations which according  to Committee are not 
practicable. The Committee in view of this recommen ds that a serious introspection is 
needed by the Central Government in this regard to avoid the problems which might emerge 
due to discontinuation of many centrally sponsored schemes.

Disaster Management 
 
 
3.5.1 Under the Head 'Disaster Management' Rs. 919. 29 crore was allocated in BE 2015-16 
which was reduced to Rs. 650.99 crore at RE stage i n that financial year.  The Ministry was asked 
about the reasons behind this decrease.   The Minis try in its written reply has informed that the 
reduction in RE 2015-16 is mainly attributable to t he delay in undertaking the works of 
development of infrastructure of various NDRF batta lions.  According to the Ministry, after EFC 
appraisal in March 2015, initiative was taken to aw ard works to the PWOs for carrying out the 
developmental activities. Due to delay in preparati on of Detailed Project Reports, the proposals 
were received in the Ministry for administrative ap proval/expenditure sanction at a very late stage. 
However, as of now, works of Office Buildings and R esidential Quarters have been awarded to 
PWOs. The utilization of funds against the administ rative sanction orders is anticipated in first 
quarter of Financial Year 2016-17. 
3.5.2 The National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project (NCRMP) is a World Bank assisted 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme with a view to address t he vulnerability of coastal community to 
cyclones who are generally poor and are from weaker  section of the society.  This project aims to 
minimize the vulnerability to cyclone and making pe ople and infrastructure disaster resilient.  The 
Ministry was asked about status of implementation o f National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project.  
The Ministry in its reply has apprised the Committe e that the project has four principal 
components namely: 
(i) Component A – Last Mile Connectivity 
(ii) Component B – Structural and Non-Structural Measures 
(iii) Component C - Technical Assistance for Cyclone Hazard Risk Mitigation,   
           Capacity Building and Knowledge Creation  
(iv) Component D – Project Management and Implementation Support. 
 

39 
 
3.5.3 According to the Ministry, Components A, C & D will be fully financed by the Central 
Government through World Bank assistance and compon ent B will be financed by Central and 
State Governments in the ratio of 75:25.   The Mini stry has also informed that the objective of the 
Project is to strengthen the structural and non str uctural mitigation infrastructure. The Project is 
being implemented with effect from January, 2011 in  the States of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha by 
NDMA at a total outlay of Rs. 1496.71 Cr. with Worl d Bank assistance to the tune of Rs. 1198.44 
Cr. (Central share) and States share to the tune of Rs. 298.27 Cr.  
 
3.5.4 The Ministry has further informed that the co st of the Project has since been revised to Rs. 
2331.71 Cr. during July, 2015 by the Government of India to reduce the infrastructural gaps 
observed during the handling of cyclones Phailin (2 013) and Hudhud (2014) by creating 
Additional Infrastructure. Now the Government of In dia will provide assistance of Rs. 1843.94 
crore through a World Bank loan and the remaining amount of Rs. 487.77 crore will be contributed 
by the State Governments of Andhra Pradesh and Odis ha. The scheme which was approved up to 
31st January, 2016 has now been extended to 31st March, 2018 with same components.  
3.5.5 According to the Ministry, till date, 232 Cyc lone Shelters, 723.48 km of roads, 19 bridges 
and 2 saline embankments have been completed under NCRMP Phase-I.  
3.5.6 Regarding NCRMP Phase-II, the Ministry has fu rnished following information:- 
(i) The Government of India has also approved Phase-II of NCRMP in July, 2015 
for implementation in the States of Goa, Gujarat, K arnataka, Kerala, 
Maharashtra and West Bengal at an outlay of Rs. 236 1.35 Cr. with the World 
Bank assistance amounting to Rs. 1881.20 Cr. The re maining amount of Rs. 
480.15 Cr. is to be contributed by State Government s as their share on the 
pattern of NCRMP Phase-I. The Project is to be impl emented by NDMA for a 
period of 5 years upto 31.03.2020.  
(ii) While the States of Gujarat and West Bengal have made physical progress in the 
matter regarding award of work for construction of shelters, the remaining 
States of Goa, Karnataka, Kerala and Maharashtra ar e in the process of 
finalization of Sites, Environment clearances, DPR, etc.  
(iii) A total of approximately Rs. 141 Cr. has been relea sed to States of Gujarat, 
Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra and West Bengal as f irst installment under 
NCRMP-II. 
(iv) The construction of 180 Cyclone Shelters and 70 Kms . roads has been awarded 
by the State of Gujarat and West Bengal under NCRMP Phase-II. 
 
3.5.7 The Ministry was also asked about measures ta ken and proposed to be taken to rehabilitate 
people affected by Chennai flood.  The Ministry in its reply submitted that the primary 
responsibility for disaster management rests with t he States and the concerned State Governments 
undertake relief & rehabilitation measures in the w ake of natural disasters from the State Disaster 
Response Fund (SDRF) already placed at their dispos al in accordance with the Government of 
India approved items and norms of assistance.  According to the Ministry, the Government of India 
supplements their efforts by providing assistance f rom the National Disaster Response Fund 

40 
 
(NDRF) by following the laid down procedure. Financ ial assistance under SDRF/NDRF in the 
wake of natural disasters is by way of relief and not for compensation of loss as suffered/claimed. 
3.5.8 The Ministry has further submitted that regar ding rehabilitation of people, who are affected 
by the natural calamities including flood, action i s undertaken by the concerned State Government 
from its own resources/Plan funds, and also based o n the availability of Government land as per 
their existing land policy and the State Government  is providing relief assistance and has taken 
initiatives to address the issue of rehabilitation as per its policy. However, the status of the 
rehabilitation measures taken by the State Government is not maintained centrally. 
3.5.9 The Ministry has also informed that in order to support the relief measures undertaken for 
the people of Tamil Nadu, affected in the recent fl ood in 2015, the Government of India had 
released an amount of Rs. 1000 crore, ‘on account’ basis from NDRF to the State Government and 
an overall amount of Rs. 2195.45 crore has been rel eased to the State to deal with the calamity so 
far.  
3.5.10 The Committee is constrained to note that Rs . 919.29 crore allocated under the Head 
'Disaster Management' in BE 2015-16 was reduced to Rs. 650.99 crore at RE stage due to 
delay in undertaking the works of development of infrastructure of various NDRF battalions.  
The Committee does not want to go into procedural wrangles leading to delay in taking off of 
any project and recommends that procedural complexi ties should be minimized to fast pace 
the project concerning development of infrastructur e of various NDRF battalions.  The 
Committee would like to be apprised of the utilisat ion status of funds in the first quarter of 
the current financial year against the administration sanction order.      
3.5.11 The Committee takes note of the mandate of W orld Bank assisted Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme National Cyclone Risk Mitigation P roject (NCRMP) whose objective is to 
address the vulnerability of coastal community to c yclones who are generally poor and are 
from weaker section of the society through minimizi ng the vulnerability to cyclone and 
making people and infrastructure disaster resilient .  The Committee hopes that this project 
will be completed in a time bound manner and go a l ong way in terms of establishing robust 
mitigation infrastructure to with stand cyclone.  T he Committee may be periodically 
apprised of the status of different projects under this scheme and also of the steps being 
taken to avoid any element of delay.  
3.5.12 The Committee is aware of the fact that the concerned affected State Governments 
have primary responsibility for disaster management  in the event of occurrence of any 
disaster and the States with their limited resource s undertake relief & rehabilitation 
measures in the wake of natural disasters.  The Com mittee recommends that the Central 
Government should play a major role in the event of  big disasters taking place in any State.   
The Committee also recommends that the Central Gove rnment should set up a monitoring 
mechanism to oversee the status of the rehabilitati on measures taken by the State 
Government without undue interference.

NATGRID  
4.2.1 It was 26/11 terror attacks on Mumbai which l ed to the exposure of several weaknesses in 
India’s intelligence gathering and action networks.   It was then came the idea  of National 
Intelligence Grid (NATGRID) which is proposed to in tegrate 21 categories of data from agencies 
like Banks, Railways and airlines, Income tax depar tment, Credit card companies Visa and 
immigration etc. This combined data will be made av ailable to 11 central agencies including the 
R&AW, NIA, CBI, Directorate of Revenue Intelligence , Intelligence Bureau, Narcotics Control 
Bureau and Enforcement Directorate to help them prevent terrorist attacks and criminal activities. 
4.2.2 The proposed National Intelligence Grid  (NAT GRID) has been set up as an attached office 
of the Ministry of Home Affairs with the mandate to  implement a framework which will leverage 
Information Technology to connect approved User Age ncies (security/law enforcement) with 
designated Data Providers (Airlines, Banks, SEBI, R ailway, Telecom, etc) with a view to enhance 
the country’s counter-terrorism capability. NATGRID will automate the existing manual processes 
for collation of intelligence information by connec ting over 80 Data Providers and develop tools 
for making actionable intelligence available to Use r Agencies. Thus, NATGRID shall be able to 
provide information online for security agencies to  save time and shall also provide actionable 
intelligence in the form of alerts & tags as defined by security agencies.  
4.2.3 The Ministry was asked about uneven trend of allocation of funds meant for NATGRID as 
in BE 2015-16 under plan allocation Rs. 52.94 crore  was allocated for NATGRID which was 
reduced to 16.81 crore at RE 2015-16 stage and agai n the Plan allocation for this project in BE 
2016-17 stands at Rs 45.00 crore.  The Ministry in its written reply has informed that in January 
2015, MHA approved a New Implementation Plan (NIP) where it was decided to implement the 
project by engaging a group of consultants and subj ect matter experts through NICSI/NISG which 
would be a more cost effective option and more cond ucive as to maintaining strategic control.  
Further, In view of rapid advancements in technology over the last few years, a need was felt to re-
evaluate the architecture and implementation method ology to ensure that a State-of-the-Art and 
optimal solution is delivered as part of NATGRID.   According to the Ministry, in light of this, an 
Advisory Group was constituted by MHA in September 2015 comprising domain experts across 
various fields to review the Detailed Project Repor t, which had been prepared in 2010.  Further, 
four sub-Committees from the members of the Advisor y Group and co-opting some additional 
members from NIC, were constituted to evaluate and suggest solutions for specific problems 
relating to technology, manpower, and implementatio n, which may confront the project during the 
course of its implementation. The meetings of sub-C ommittees have since been completed and the 
recommendations are being placed before the Advisor y Group. Due to this reason, the project 
implementation has been delayed, resulting in reduction in RE 2015-16 from BE 2015-16.   
4.2.4 The Committee is aware that NATGRID was conce ived after the 2008 Mumbai 
Terror Attack which many in security establishments  believe, could have been averted but 
for delayed scattered intelligence.  It aims to bri ng to one platform intelligence from over 
20 agencies like railways, banks, IB, RAW, CBI, ED,  Central Board of Direct Taxes, etc.  
The NATRGID is expected to use cutting edge technol ogy to place all the details regarding 
telephone, residential, travel and banking of a sus pect on a common platform. However, 
the Committee is extremely disappointed at the slow progress.  NATGRID was conceived in 
2010-11 to be put in place in four phases.  Two pha ses were planned to be completed by 

49 
 
2014 at an estimated cost of Rs. 1100 crore.  It is disheartening to know that even phase one 
has not been completed till date.  
 
4.2.5 The Committee is also aware that construction  of a building to house NATGRID 
was given to NBCC after foundation stone was laid i n 2014 in South Delhi.  It has taken 
around 2 years to get clearance from the State Leve l Environment Impact Assessment 
Authority (SLEIAA), which was granted in November, 2015.  Though as per the Ministry's 
information, construction has begun w.e.f February,  2016,   the estimated cost of the 
proposed complex is Rs. 150 crore but the total bud get allocation in 2016-17 is only Rs. 45 
crore.  It is very clear to the Committee that Gove rnment has gone slow on the NATGRID 
project whereas it strongly feels that his project should be given priority in order to tackle 
high-tech terrorism which has become order of the d ay. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry must prepare a plan wi th clear timeframe within which all 
the four phases should be completed as per set targ et and if required, the Ministry should 
ask for enhanced allocation at RE stage.   
 
4.2.6 The Ministry was asked to inform the Committe e about projected demand of the Ministry 
for NATGRID.  The Ministry in its response apprised  the Committee that MHA had projected for 
year 2016-17 Rs.104.00 crore, out of which Rs.45.00  Cr is under the Revenue Section and the 
Capital Head ‘M&E’, and Rs.59.00 crores was under t he Capital Head “Major Works” grouped 
separately under the Head ‘13.Police Infrastructure  13.01 CAPFs and Central Police 
Organizations' in the Expenditure Budget 2016-17 (V olume 2- Notes on Demands for Grants). 
According to the Ministry, the demand for “Major Wo rks” is a conservative demand, keeping in 
view the earlier trend of savings in BE.  The Minis try has further apprised that the construction 
work at New Delhi will pick up and any additional f unds required in 2016-17 would be sought 
through Supplementary Demands for Grants.  
4.2.7 The Ministry has given details of the progres s on this project .  According to the Ministry, 
NATGRID Scheme has two sub-projects. One sub projec t aims at setting up of the NATGRID IT 
framework/solution, and the other one for establishment of the physical infrastructure on which the 
NATGRID IT framework will be hosted – consisting of Data Centre, Business Continuity Plan and 
Office Complex at New Delhi, Disaster Recovery Centre at Bengaluru.  
4.2.8 The Ministry has submitted that CCS in June, 2012 approved implementation of Horizon I 
and some elements of Horizon II of the IT Framework  sub-project envisaged in the Detailed 
Project Report (DPR) for an estimated cost of Rs. 1 002.97 Cr, which were to be implemented in a 
period of 24 months from the CCS approval.  Accordi ng the Ministry Project implementation 
period has been further extended up to 30th June, 2 017.   The status of sub-projects and measures 
taken for their speedy implementation are as below: 
 
a) The deployment of complete solution can commence on ly after the physical 
construction of Data Centre(s) at New Delhi and Ben galuru. As per the high 
security/privacy norms mandated by the CCS – NATGRI D’s Data Centre, Disaster 
Recovery Centre and Business Continuity Plan site a re central to NATGRID’s 
capability to securely store critical data and serv ice the User Agencies through high 
security channels. NATGRID was instructed that thes e facilities will have to be 

50 
 
constructed by National Building Corporation Compan y (NBCC) on a turnkey basis. 
While the civil construction at Bangalore site is g oing as per schedule and is likely to 
be completed by June, 2016, the construction at Del hi site could not start as South 
Delhi Municipal Corporation (SDMC) disputed Delhi D evelopment Authority 
(DDA)ownership of the land. The issue between DDA a nd SDMC has been resolved. 
After the transfer in July 2015 to SDMC the land co st of Rs.19.29 Cr paid to DDA in 
earlier years and further payment of the additional  land cost to SDMC of Rs.11.01 Cr 
on 28.12.2015, the allotted land has been handed ov er to NATGRID on 31.12.2015. 
The construction has started in February 2016. 
 
b) In view of rapid advancements in technology over th e last few years, a need was felt to 
re-evaluate the architecture and implementation met hodology for the IT Framework 
sub-project as proposed in the NATGRID DPR,which wa s prepared in 2010, to ensure 
that a State-of-the-Art and optimal solution is del ivered as part of NATGRID. In light 
of this, an Advisory Group was constituted by MHA i n September 2015 comprising 
domain experts across various fields to review the DPR. Further, four sub-Committees 
from the members of the Advisory Group and co-opting some additional members from 
NIC, were constituted to evaluate and suggest solut ions for specific problems relating 
to technology, manpower, and implementation, which may confront the project during 
the course of its implementation. The meetings of s ub-Committees have since been 
completed and the recommendations are being placed before the Advisory Group. 
 
c) Further to the approval of a New Implementation Pla n by MHA in January 2015, 
whereby it has been envisaged to implement the IT F ramework sub-project directly by 
NATGRID with the help of a group of consultants and subject matter experts, in a more 
cost-effective manner and more conducive to maintai ning strategic controls compared 
to the earlier decision to engage a Project Managem ent Consultant for implementation 
of the sub-project, approval has been accorded by M HA in December 2015 for 
engagement of National Institute of Smart Governmen t (NISG) to provide to 
NATGRID 40 consultants. The detailed modalities of on-boarding the consultants are 
being finalised. 
 
4.2.9 The Committee is given to understand that NAT GRID aims to enhance the country’s 
counter-terrorism capability through sharing inform ation online and providing actionable 
intelligence.  The Committee while noting the reply  of the Ministry, justifying uneven trend 
of allocation of funds meant for NATGRID since last  financial year, hopes that New 
Implementation Plan (NIP) as envisaged would prove to be successful experiment in terms of 
cost effectiveness and conducive to maintain strategic control. Since this project is of national 
importance in terms of ensuring internal security o f this country, the Committee also 
recommends that bureaucratic red-tapism should be k ept at minimum to check procedural 
delay without compromising quality in implementatio n of this project.  Besides, the 
Government should make allocation as per requiremen t to help erecting necessary physical 
infrastructure and make NATGRID functional at the earliest.

Border Area Development Programme (BADP) 
 
4.6.1 The main objective of the BADP is to meet the  special developmental needs and well being 
of the people living in remote and inaccessible are as situated near the international border and to 
saturate the border areas with the entire essential  infrastructure through convergence of 
Central/State/ BADP/Local schemes and participatory  approach. BADP covers 391 border blocks 
of 106 border districts in 17 States viz. Arunachal  Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Gujarat, Himachal 
Pradesh, Jammu &Kashmir, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizora m, Nagaland, Punjab, Rajasthan, 
Sikkim, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Wes t Bengal.  The BADP is supplemental in 
nature to fill the gaps. Funds under BADP are provi ded to the States as a 100% non-lapsable 

58 
 
Special Central Assistance. The schemes/works under taken under the BADP relate to construction 
of roads, bridges, safe drinking water supply, heal th, agriculture and allied activities, social secto r 
such as social infrastructure, capacity building an d skill development, Swatchhta Abhiyan, 
construction of toilets particularly for women,  ed ucation, sports activities, promotion of rural 
tourism/border tourism, etc.    
 4.6.2  The Ministry was asked about projected dema nds of the Ministry for BADP for this 
financial year and if it is adequate or not. In response, ministry has apprised that over the years, the 
development of border areas has become a priority o f the Central Government but the fund 
allocation of the BADP has been grossly inadequate to cater to the needs of the border population. 
According to the Ministry, on the other hand, the S tate Governments perceived development of 
border areas as the responsibility and priority of the Central Government and a very little effort has 
been made to fund these areas through State Plan so urces or to converge funds available under the 
CSS which led to a big gap between the pace of deve lopment in the border villages and the 
hinterland. 
4.6.3 The Ministry has further submitted that the b udgetary allocation for BADP for the financial 
year (2016-17) has been fixed as Rs. 990 crore agai nst a demand of Rs. 1800.00 crore and thus, it  
is grossly inadequate to meet the developmental nee d of the border population to arrest their 
migration from the remote border areas, in search of better lively hood in other developed areas. 
4.6.4 The BADP allocation for during the last three  years given as under: 
/square4 2013-14: Rs. 990.00  Crore 
/square4 2014-15: Rs. 800.00 Crore  (RE) 
/square4 2015-16: Rs. 990.00 Crore 
 
4.6.5 The Ministry has submitted that the border ar eas need massive funds for development to 
make border people self-reliant and to bring them a t par with other developed parts of the country 
to stop migration of people from the border areas.  
4.6.6    The allocation for Border Area Development  Programme (BADP) under Plan scheme in 
BE 2016-17 is to the tune of Rs. 990.00 crore.  Reg arding utilization of this amount, the Ministry 
has informed that as per the BADP guidelines  the b udgetary allocation shall be divided into two 
component- viz.(i) First component being  40% of to tal budgetary allocation for the eight  North-
Eastern (NE) States (including Sikkim); and (ii) re maining 60% of total allocation for the States 
other than the eight NE States on the basis of (i) Length of International border; (ii) Population of 
the Border Blocks; (iii) Area of the Border blocks (all the above three criteria shall have equal 
weightage). 15% weightage will be given to hilly /desert and Ra nn of Kutch area on account of 
difficult terrain and scarcity of resources and hig her cost of construction. The smaller States which 
have less International Border and small population  shall be given fixed allocation.  The State 
Governments shall manage the funds, within the allo cation made to the States as per the above 
formula, for the villages located within  the permi ssible distance from the international land border 
but are not in the blocks which touch the international border.  
4.6.7 The Committee notes submission of the Ministr y that Border Area Development 
Programme aims to meet the special developmental ne eds and well being of the people living 

59 
 
in remote and inaccessible areas situated near the international border through construction 
of physical and social infrastructure.  The Committ ee, however, is constrained to note that 
over the years the fund allocation of the BADP has been grossly inadequate to cater to the 
needs of the border population and the Centre is sh irking its responsibility.   It is also noted 
that the budgetary allocation for BADP for the fina ncial year (2016-17) is Rs. 990 crore 
against projected demand of Rs. 1800.00 crore which  is almost half of the projection.  The 
Committee is of the strong opinion that the develop ment of border areas should not suffer 
for want of funds and therefore recommends that the  allocation may be enhanced at RE 
stage to meet the developmental need of the populac e residing in border areas to check their 
migration from there.   The Committee also recommen ds that the share of BSF under the 
allocation meant for BADP should be increased from mere 10% to at least 40% as they are 
the people who happen to be well versed with the pr oblems faced by populace living in 
border areas and moreover they are much accessible to the people of border areas.

and the effort of the Central Government has been t o meet the gap between requirement and 
availability of  funds at the disposal of the State  Govt. for modernisation of Police forces on

Force (MPF) Scheme was reviewed by the High Powered  Committee in the Ministry of Home

states as it has achieved its objectives.  
4.9.4 According to the Ministry, during the fourtee n years from 2000-01 to 2013-14, against a 
total amount of Rs. 13,749.82 crore released under the MPF Scheme, the States had utilized Rs.

total amount of Rs. 825.13 crore have been released  to States/UTs upto 3 rd  March, 2016. Out of 
this, Rs. 698.43 crore have been utilized by them w hich is 85% of the total funds released. States 
are regularly advised for timely utilization of funds. 
4.9.5 The allocation on Special infrastructure for LWE areas has not been made in BE 2016-17 
like last financial year.   The Ministry was asked about rationale behind this decision.  The 
Ministry in its reply has submitted that Special In frastructure Scheme (SIS), was being 
implemented since 2008-09 in LWE affected States fo r providing central assistance to States for 
filling up critical infrastructure gaps of their sp ecial security forces, which could not be covered 
under any other existing scheme.    According to th e Ministry, during 11 th  Plan period (2008-09 to 
2011-12), Rs. 445.82 crore and during 12 th  Plan period (2013-14 and 2014-15), Rs. 122.13 cror e 
has been released to the LWE affected States under the Scheme. 
 4.9.6 The Ministry has further submitted that acce pting the recommendations of the 14 th  Finance 
Commission to enhance the share of States in the ne t proceeds of Union taxes from 32% to 42%, 
the Government has delinked the SIS from Central as sistance from 2015-16. The scheme has been 
transferred to the States for giving them sufficien t flexibility to conceive and implement 
schemes/programmes suited to their local needs, inc luding requirements to bridge the 
developmental deficit gaps , hence, no fund has bee n allocated in BE 2016-17 under the Scheme. 
The scheme was useful for training infrastructure, residential infrastructure, weaponry, vehicles 
and any other related items pertaining to the upgra dation and filling of critical gaps for Special 
Forces of LWE affected States.  
4.9.7 In view of the importance of the Scheme, the Committee was informed that MHA has 
proposed to revive this scheme as a component of Um brella Scheme namely, ‘Modernization of 
Police Forces’ of the Central Government from 2016- 17 in consultation with the Department of 
Expenditure.                                                                                                                                                
4.9.8 The Committee notes that Rs. 1753.90 crore ha s been allocated in BE 2016-17 which is 
a steep rise as compared with Rs. 662.11 crore as a llocated in RE 2015-16 under this scheme. 
The Committee also notes submission of the Ministry  that increased allocation is on account 
of consolidation of the some schemes under the Umbr ella Scheme of Modernization of Police 
Forces.  The Committee, however, understands that e ven this increased allocation is not as 
per requirement of the States.  The Committee is of  the view that the State Governments 
require large sum of allocation to modernize their police forces, to improve police 
infrastructure and to launch development initiative s in the Left Wing Extremist affected 
areas.  In view of the above, the Committee recomme nds that big enhancement should be

under the scheme "Modernisation of Police Forces". Besides, no allocation has been made

4.9.9 The Committee further notes that "The Mega Ci ty Policing", a sub-set of the Non-

CHAPTER - VI 
PATHANKOT AIRBASE ATTACK  
 
BACKGROUND  
 
6.1.1 On the 2 nd  January 2016, a heavily armed terror group attacke d the Pathankot Air Force 
Station, located in the State of Punjab which is part of the Western Air Command of the Indian Air 
Force. In the counter terror operation by Indian se curity agencies, four attackers and two security 
forces personnel were killed and five more security personnel died of injuries.    
6.1.2 Furnishing the details of how the attack unfo lded, the Ministry has submitted in writing 
which is as under:- 
"In this background, in the early morning of 1 st  January, 2016 at around 03.23 a.m., 
the Police Control Room, Gurdaspur received information from Shri Salvinder Singh, 
an Addl. SP rank officer of the Punjab Police poste d in 75 th  Battalion of Punjab 
Armed Police, that some unidentified persons in mil itary uniforms had hijacked his 
vehicle and kidnapped him along with his friend, Sh ri Rajesh Verma, and orderly, 
Shri Madan Gopal from Village Kohlian in the area o f PS Narot Jaimal Singh, 
District Pathankot, and subsequently he and his ord erly were thrown out of the 
vehicle near Gulpur Simbli in the area of PS Kanwan . This information was passed 
on to Pathankot Control Room of Punjab Police by th e Gurdaspur Control Room of 
Punjab Police. A red alert was sounded by the Punja b Police in Pathankot District 
and the adjoining Gurdaspur District after the rece ipt of this information. 
Subsequently, Shri Rajesh Verma was traced to Amand eep Hospital, Pathankot, with 
severe injuries inflicted on him by the abductors, who had abandoned him in Village 
Bellian, PS Sadar Pathankot. The Punjab Police laun ched a search for the vehicle of 
Shri Salvinder Singh, which was found abandoned in the fields of Village Tajpur in 
the area of PS Sadar, Pathankot.During the examinat ion of Shri Rajesh Verma by the 
police, it was disclosed that the abductors were ta lking among themselves about 
attacking some defence establishment. It was also disclosed that two mobile phones of 
Shri Salvinder Singh and one mobile phone of Shri R ajesh Verma were also robbed 
by the abductors. Based on this information, the of ficers of various agencies, 
including the Intelligence Bureau, Military Intelli gence, Punjab Police, etc., had 
arrived at the conclusion that the abductors are te rrorists, planning an attack on a 
military establishment."

th  January, 2016, the Chairman asked the 
Home Secretary to apprise the Committee, in the fir st instance with the latest status on the terror 
attack in Pathankot. The Home Secretary then appris ing the Committee on the happenings in 
Pathankot, informed the Committee that while the te rrorists had been neutralized, the combing 
operations were going on to sanitize the complete a rea.   The submission of Home Secretary is as 
follows:-

 " ................, Sir, basically, some terrorist s, who are still to be identified by name or

6.1.4 During its study visit to western border area s in Punjab and Rajasthan, the Committee

OPERATION TO NEUTRALISE TERRORISTS  
6.2.1 The Ministry was asked about  action taken by the Central Government on the intel ligence 
inputs received.  The Ministry in response apprised  the Committee that the information regarding 
attack was shared by the Punjab Police with the cen tral agencies and the local Army and Air Force 
officials and thereafter, the interception of the m obile numbers robbed by the terrorists disclosed 
that they were planning an attack on a defence esta blishment and, accordingly, security was put on 
high alert in the nearby defence establishments. 
6.2.2 According to the Ministry, on the basis of th e above information, a meeting of senior 
officers was convened by the Central Government and  consequent to the meeting, the Army Units 
were mobilized, Air Force Commando Garuds were flow n along with Air Officer Commander in 
Chief, Western Command and the NSG was airlifted to  the most possible target of terror attack, 
the Air Force Station, Pathankot, by the evening of 1 
st  January, 2016.   The Ministry has added that 
as a precautionary measure, high value air assets w ere moved away from the Airbase and 
subsequently, Army also inducted Special Forces (1 Para) Bomb Disposal Units and other 
specialized equipments.   
 
6.2.3 Countering the allegation of lack of coordina tion between different police and security 
forces before and during the Pathankot terror attac k as reported in the media, the Ministry has 
submitted that due to the intelligence inputs made available consequent to the abduction of Shri 
Salvinder Singh and the interception of communicati on between the terrorists and their handlers, a 

111 
 
well planned, well-coordinated anti-terrorist operation was launched by the security forces and due 
to  real time mobilization and deployment, all the terrorists involved in the attack were neutralized 
without any loss of assets of the Indian Air force,  which was the main target of attack by the 
terrorists.  There was clear chain of command and control during the operation. 
6.2.4 The Ministry was asked to provide a timeline of sequence of events before and during the 
attack w.r.t.  infiltration, entry into airbase, at tack and damage by the terrorists and operation to 
neutralise them.  The Ministry in its response has stated that this aspect is under investigation by 
the NIA. 
6.2.5 There were reports that some of the terrorist s/infiltrators who were not neutralised managed 
to escape after the Pathankot attack.  The Ministry  was asked about facts in this regard.  The 
Ministry has informed the Committee that all the te rrorists involved in the Pathankot airbase terror 
attack were neutralized by the security forces.  
6.2.6 First of all, the Committee is unable to unde rstand that in spite of terror alert 
sounded well in advance, how terrorists managed to breach the high-security air base and 
subsequently made attack.  The Committee is constra ined to note that despite concrete and 
credible intelligence inputs received from abducted and released Pathankot’s Superintendent 
of Police (SP) and his friend and through intercept ion of communication between terrorists 
and their handlers by the terrorists disclosing that they were planning an attack on a defence 
establishment, the security agencies of our country  were so ill-prepared 
to anticipate threats 
in time and counter them swiftly and decisively. 
6.2.7 The Committee feels that something is serious ly wrong with our counter-terror 
security establishment. Despite the fencing, floodl ighting and patrolling by BSF personnel, 
Pakistani terrorists managed to sneak into India fr om across the border.  The Committee 
understands that  in this attack, the role of Punja b Police is also very questionable and 
suspicious as even after abduction of Punjab Police  SP, the Punjab Police took longtime in 
arriving at the conclusion that their abduction was  not just a criminal robbery but it was 
going to be serious national security threat. The C ommittee is unable to understand why the 
terrorists let the SP and his friend off, which sho uld be thoroughly examined by NIA.  
Besides, the Committee is of the view that the role  of narco-syndicate active in border areas 
of Punjab should also be investigated as the terror ists might have taken help of channels or 
networks used by smugglers to infiltrate the border, shelter and  carry out terror attack. 
6.2.8 The Committee also recommends that in view of  the series of attacks from across the 
international border in this area, the Government o f India should pay attention to effectively 
sealing the border through enhanced patrolling, fencing, flood lighting, etc.  
6.2.9 The Committee during its visit found that air base’s security cover was not robust and 
it had a poorly guarded perimeter wall.  The perime ter wall of airbase was not having   
patrolling road around it. The Committee also found growth of long shrubs and trees in the 
premises which might have helped terrorists in hidi ng and making difficult for security 
forces in combing out these terrorists.  The Commit tee recommends that the Pathankot 
Airbase which is very close to border should be dec lared high security zone and should be 

112 
 
properly secured through round the clock patrolling and making it out of bounds for general 
people residing around the airbase. 
FOREIGN HAND BEHIND THE ATTACK 
 
6.3.1 There were speculations of terrorist attack o n Pathankot Air Force base sponsored by 
elements in Pakistan.  The Ministry was asked about authenticity of this Report. The Ministry in its 
written reply informed the Committee that Indian In telligence agencies have been receiving inputs 
indicating efforts by terrorist outfit, Jaish-e-Moh ammad, led by Maulana Masood Azhar to 
infiltrate into India from Pakistan territory to ca rry out terrorist attack on Defence / Police 
establishments in India and such intelligence input s were shared with all the stakeholders 
concerned and there was a heightened security alert.   
6.3.2 In view of the Committee, there cannot be no two opinion on the fact that Pakistan 
based Jaish-e-Mohammad terror group  was behind this ghastly terror attack which was 
established through interception of calls between t errorists and their handlers based in 
Pakistan, thanks to their use of robbed mobile phones from Pathankot SP  and his friend.  
Besides, weapons, ammunitions and many items found in posses sion of killed terrorists are 
also said to be having 'Made in Pakistan' marking.  
6.3.3 In view of the ease with which the terrorists  sneaked into our side from Pakistan, the 
Committee understands that the attack cannot take p lace without active support from  
security and intelligence agencies of Pakistan as  four  armed men cannot easily pass through 
heavy Pakistani defence establishment situated  near border area.

6.4.1 On the question of progress made in the inves tigation of the incident of Pathankot Airbase
